Only SCMs support counterfactuals, because “to compute counterfactuals, we need to fix the value of the noise variables.” Many different combinations of function and noise produce the same conditional distribution, so a causal graph with its conditionals isn’t enough on its own.
(Background.) Pearl’s standard three-step recipe for counterfactuals spells out what “fixing the noise” means: 1. Abduction: from what actually happened, infer this case’s noise values. 2. Action: apply the hypothetical intervention. 3. Prediction: recompute the outcome with the same noise values.
Causal learning and reasoning. Statistical learning works with a joint distribution and assumptions about function classes. Causal learning also uses the causal factorization and the interventions it admits. Given a causal model (learned or supplied by experts), causal reasoning answers questions about interventions, counterfactuals, and potential outcomes.
In plain words. A causal graph tells you which way the influence flows, which is enough for “what happens on average if we do X?” A counterfactual about one specific person also needs that person’s individual quirks: their noise terms. An SCM keeps track of those, so it can replay the same person’s story with one thing changed.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Slides: “The ICM Principle”, “Example: Altitude and Temperature”, “The Sparse Mechanism Shift (SMS) Hypothesis”.


The idea. Our visual system assumes that an object is independent of the light falling on it, of our viewpoint, and of the illumination. This is the generic viewpoint assumption: no accidental coincidences, such as 3D structures lining up perfectly in a 2D image or shadow edges landing exactly on texture edges. When such coincidences do happen, we see optical illusions. Structure from motion relies on the same idea: moving around an object changes the viewpoint while lighting, position, and shape stay the same, which lets us infer 3D shape even with one eye.
In plain words. Your brain bets that “what the thing is” and “how you’re looking at it” are separate facts. That bet is usually right, and when it’s wrong you get an optical illusion.



The idea. Altitude \(A\) of weather stations causes their average annual temperature \(T\). Data from Austria and from Switzerland have different joint distributions \(P(A, T)\), because the distribution of station altitudes \(P(A)\) differs. But \(P(T \mid A)\) encodes physics and should be nearly the same in both.

Causal factorization \(P(A)\,P(T \mid A)\): one factor changes by country, the other generalizes.
Entangled factorization \(P(T)\,P(A \mid T)\): both factors mix geography with physics, so both change.

Without knowing the causal structure, the cross-country similarity is lost.
In plain words. Air gets colder as you climb at the same rate in every country. What differs is how many mountains each country has. Store your knowledge as “how many mountains here” plus “how cold it gets with height,” and you only update the first part when you travel. Store it the other way round, and both parts are wrong in the new country.



The idea. The causal generative process of a system’s variables is “composed of autonomous modules that do not inform or influence each other.” For the causal factorization this means:

(a) Influence: changing one mechanism \(P(X_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\) does not change any other mechanism.
(b) Information: knowing some mechanisms tells you nothing about the others.

This entails that causal variables can be intervened on separately, that subsystems are modular and autonomous, and that mechanisms are invariant. With two variables, it says the distribution of the cause is independent of the mechanism that produces the effect from it.
Two clarifications from the paper: - Independent mechanisms ≠ independent variables. Variables can be strongly dependent even when all mechanisms are independent. Independence of the noise terms \(U_i\) is a special case of ICM. - Algorithmic formulation. Because statistical information is awkward to define for deterministic mechanisms, the paper also states ICM in terms of Kolmogorov complexity (the length of the shortest program that outputs a string). Write each mechanism as a bit string; the mechanisms are independent if “joint compression of these strings does not save space relative to independent compressions,” i.e. their mutual algorithmic information is zero. In such algorithmic graphical models, each \(X_i\) is the output of a fixed computer running program \(U_i\) on input \(\mathbf{PA}_i\), and analogues of the Markov condition and the causal factorization still hold. The paper concludes that “causality is not intrinsically bound to statistics.”
History. The idea has deep roots: Haavelmo (1944) assumed that changing one structural equation leaves the others intact; Simon’s invariance criterion holds that the true causal order is invariant under the right interventions; Aldrich (1989) quotes Frisch asking of a relation “How autonomous is it?”; Pearl (2009) notes that causal discovery works under slightly varying conditions, where accidental independencies break but structural ones persist.
In plain words. Nature is built from separate, swappable parts. (a) Changing one part doesn’t break the others: replacing a car’s tyres doesn’t change how the engine works. (b) Studying one part tells you nothing about another: the tyre brand gives no clue about engine design. The compression version says the same thing: if two rules are truly separate, describing them together takes no less space than describing them one at a time.



The idea. “Small distribution changes tend to manifest themselves in a sparse or local way in the causal/disentangled factorization.” They should usually not affect all factors at once. Since every real-world distribution is a product of causal mechanisms, any change must come from a change in at least one mechanism. In an entangled factorization, by contrast, a single change typically spreads across many or all terms.
The paper notes that SMS has been used as a learning signal: for learning causal models, for modular architectures, and for disentanglement. If the right representation is the one under which observed shifts look sparse, then searching for sparse-shift representations gives supervision that doesn’t need labels.
In plain words. When something changes in the world, usually only one or two things actually change. A lab installs a new microscope; patient biology stays the same. If your model is organised the right way, that change shows up as one small edit. If it’s organised the wrong way, it shows up as a mess everywhere. So “which description makes changes look small and local?” is a clue to the right description.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Slide: “Causal Discovery Meets ML”.


The idea. Under assumptions such as faithfulness, conditional independence (CI) tests recover part of the graph from observational data, up to its Markov equivalence class: graphs with the same skeleton (edges without directions) and the same immoralities (\(X_i \to X_j \leftarrow X_k\) with \(X_i\) and \(X_k\) not directly connected).
Two problems: 1. CI testing is hard with finite data, especially with continuous, multi-dimensional conditioning sets. Kernel methods are the main modern approach. 2. With only two variables there are no conditional independencies to test, so the Markov condition says nothing about direction.
(Background.) Faithfulness means every independence in the data is implied by the graph, not produced by a coincidental cancellation of effects. The paper cites but does not define it.
In plain words. CI tests are detective work: “if A and C stop being related once I know B, then B probably sits between them.” This only narrows things down to a family of candidate graphs, needs lots of data, and doesn’t work at all for a single pair of variables.



The idea. Both problems can be addressed by restricting the class of functions, which is where ML’s learning theory comes in. In the general model \(X := U\), \(Y := f(X, V)\), the noise \(V\) can select among arbitrarily different functions, so a finite sample says little. The additive noise model (ANM) restricts this:
\[X := U, \qquad Y := f(X) + V, \qquad U \perp\!\!\!\perp V.\]
Key result: given data from an ANM in one direction, you generically cannot fit an ANM in the reverse direction. That breaks the symmetry between cause and effect. The exception is the linear case with Gaussian noise, where both directions fit equally well. Extensions cover linear non-Gaussian models (LiNGAM), non-linear rescalings, loops, confounders, and multivariate settings. Other methods that beat chance at finding direction use compression, generative networks, or train a classifier to label pairs of variables as cause→effect or effect→cause.
In plain words. If \(Y\) is “a function of \(X\) plus independent random wobble,” then trying to explain \(X\) from \(Y\) leaves wobble that does depend on \(Y\). That mismatch gives away the wrong direction. If everything is linear and bell-curve shaped, the fingerprint disappears.



The idea. Under SMS, most of the causal structure stays fixed across shifts. So observing a system in several environments or contexts can reveal causal structure. Contexts can come from interventions, non-stationary time series, or multiple views of the same system. Contexts can also be tasks, which links causal discovery to meta-learning: - Bengio et al. relate meta-learning to causal invariance: a correct causal model should adapt faster to an intervention than a merely predictive one. - Ke et al. extend this to many variables and unknown interventions, turning the discrete search over graphs into continuous optimization. - Dasgupta et al. have an RL agent learn a causal model.
All of these still assume the meaningful variables are given; none learns them from pixels.
In plain words. Data from several settings works like a natural experiment: whatever stays stable across settings is likely a real mechanism. And the right causal model is the one that needs the fewest adjustments when the setting changes, so “adapts fastest” is itself a clue.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Slides: “The Setting: Causal Variables Aren’t Given”, “Problem Formulation”, “SMS in Pixel Space”, “Three Problems for CRL”.


The idea. Causal discovery assumes its units are random variables already connected by a graph. Real observations aren’t structured that way; images don’t come labelled with their objects. Fig. 2 describes perceptual data as “entangled views of the state of an unknown causal system,” usually with no labels except perhaps a task label. Full recovery of the causal system may be unrealistic, so the aim is a representation that exposes enough causal structure to support causal statements for downstream tasks. Example: to detect objects a robot could manipulate, separate an object’s intrinsic properties from its pose and appearance, so the detector is robust when pose and appearance shift.
Choosing the level of description (granularity) is hard. Fields like economics, medicine, and psychology use coarse variables whose interventions are not well defined. Causal variables can be coarse-grained summaries of finer models (microscopic equations, ODEs, time series aggregated over time).
The paper’s proposed architecture: embed an SCM inside a larger neural network whose inputs and outputs are high-dimensional. Its modules can then be fine-tuned and reused, and SMS can be used to shape the structure.
In plain words. A camera doesn’t record “ball,” “table,” “gravity.” It records a million coloured dots. Causal tools need the ball and the table as named things. Causal representation learning is about getting from the dots to the things, choosing things that actually cause one another.



The idea. Observations \(X\) (say, an image with \(d\) pixels) are generated from \(n \ll d\) latent causal variables through a non-linear map \(G\):
\[X = G(S_1, \dots, S_n), \qquad S_i := f_i(\mathbf{PA}_i, U_i), \qquad P(S_1, \dots, S_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(S_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i).\]
Architecture: an autoencoder with an SCM in the bottleneck. - An encoder \(q: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^n\) maps \(X\) to noise variables \(U_1, \dots, U_n\). - The causal mechanisms \(f\) turn noises into causal variables \(S_1, \dots, S_n\). - A decoder \(p: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^d\) maps the causal variables back to an image. - Train by reconstruction error so that \(p \circ f \circ q \approx \mathrm{id}\).
If the graph is known, \(f\)’s structure can be fixed. If not, \(f\) gets absorbed into the decoder (\(\tilde p = p \circ f\)), and the causal graph is implicit in the decoder. Leeb et al. propose a structured decoder along these lines.
The catch is identifiability. From i.i.d. data alone, recovering the true noise variables is ill-defined: infinitely many solutions give the same observational distribution. Extra inductive biases are needed to prefer the right one.
In plain words. Compress an image into a few causal “knobs,” let the knobs influence each other according to learned cause-and-effect rules, then redraw the image. If the redrawing matches, the knobs capture what matters. The problem is that many different sets of knobs redraw the image equally well, and nothing in the images alone forces the true causal ones. Extra hints are needed, such as data from changing environments.



The idea. Fig. 3 shows an intervention (“which may or may not be intentional/observed”) that moves one finger of a robotic hand; as a consequence, an object (a cube) falls. In the right causal variables the change is sparse: the finger’s position changed, and the cube’s position changed as a result. In pixel space the change is dense, or entangled: many pixels change at once. In the extreme, “all pixels may change as a result of a sparse intervention,” for example if the camera angle or lighting changes.
In plain words. To a camera, a cube falling off a hand changes much of the picture. To a person, only one thing happened: a finger moved and gravity did the rest. A good representation sees it the way the person does.



The idea. Find an encoder whose latent variables satisfy the disentangled factorization \(\prod_i P(S_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\), with each conditional separately manipulable and largely invariant across related problems.

Most disentanglement work assumes fully independent factors, the special case where every \(\mathbf{PA}_i\) is empty. ICM is more general: a fork and a knife are statistically dependent (they appear together), yet we want them as separate entities.
Object-centric representations are another special case: objects can be intervened on separately, so they make natural building blocks, complemented by orientation, viewpoint, and lighting.
To make the latents causal, use ICM: independent noises and independent mechanisms, enforced through invariance across problems, sparse changes, or independent interventions.
Locatello et al. showed that SMS is theoretically sufficient for disentanglement given suitable training data. SMS can supervise learning even when variables have parents.
Which factors can be disentangled depends on which interventions are observed; different supervision signals identify different subsets of factors.

In plain words. Learn separate knobs for separate real-world factors, so turning one doesn’t secretly turn others, and use “the world changed, but only a little” as the clue for where the knobs are.



The idea. Real agents have limited data and limited compute (brains have a size limit; robots run on batteries). They can’t rely on “large-scale labeling work done by humans.” So robust AI will need to reuse components across tasks and environments, ideally with a modular structure that mirrors the world’s modularity.
The paper’s lighting example: a visual system shouldn’t train a separate face recogniser for each lighting condition. It should have a gain-control module that factors out lighting variations spanning orders of magnitude. That module need not mimic the physics of light, but it plays the corresponding role, which may push models toward a structure that mirrors the world. Looking for independent mechanisms, possibly through competitive training between modules, is a sensible inductive bias.
In plain words. Build a toolkit of reusable parts instead of a custom machine for every job. One “adjust for brightness” tool serves every face, every room, every task.



The idea. Deep learning captures statistics but “does not care about the interventional properties of the variables it analyzes or reconstructs.” Causal representation learning should produce models that support “intervention, planning, and reasoning,” realizing Lorenz’s thinking as acting in an imagined space. That requires reflecting on one’s actions and imagining alternatives, possibly needing “(the illusion of) free will.” The paper speculates that self-consciousness may relate to having a variable that represents oneself in that imagined space, and that free will may be a way to communicate about actions, which matters for social and cultural learning.
In plain words. The model should let an agent imagine “if I push this, that happens” before doing it, the way people rehearse actions in their heads, including picturing themselves in the scene.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Slides: “Semi-Supervised Learning”, “Adversarial Examples and Robustness”, “Re-reading Today’s Tricks”, “Science, Medicine and Multi-Task Learning”.
The paper drops the i.i.d. assumption and assumes test data may come from a different distribution “but involving (mostly) the same causal mechanisms.” It names four challenges:


abstract causal variables often have to be inferred from low-level inputs;


there is no consensus on which aspects of data reveal causal relations;


the usual train/test protocol may be insufficient, and new benchmarks may need environment information and interventions;


scalable, numerically sound algorithms are often missing.




The idea. - Causal direction \(X \to Y\): \(P(X, Y) = P(X)\,P(Y \mid X)\). By ICM, \(P(X)\) carries no information about \(P(Y \mid X)\), so semi-supervised learning (SSL) should be futile, to the extent it relies on unlabeled data about \(P(X)\) to improve \(P(Y \mid X)\). - Anticausal direction \(Y \to X\) (predicting against the generative direction): Daniušis et al. define a measure of dependence between \(P(X)\) and \(P(Y \mid X)\) that is zero in the causal direction but strictly positive in the anticausal one. So unlabeled \(X\) carries information about the conditional, and SSL can work.
The study Schölkopf et al. (2012), On Causal and Anticausal Learning, “empirically corroborated these predictions”, and about 17 follow-up papers built on it. The idea also inspired invariance-based causal discovery in statistics.
The standard SSL assumptions fit this picture: the cluster assumption (labels don’t change within a cluster of \(P(X)\)), low-density separation (the decision boundary lies where \(P(X)\) is small), and semi-supervised smoothness. Co-training assumes two views are independent given the label, exactly what you expect when the label causes both views, an anticausal setting.
(Background examples.) Causal: predicting a protein from its mRNA sequence. Anticausal: classifying a handwritten digit from its image, where the intended digit causes the ink.
In plain words. If the label causes the input (the writer chose “7” and then drew it), then piles of unlabeled images naturally fall into clusters, one per digit, and those clusters help draw boundaries. If the input causes the label, the way inputs are spread out says nothing about the rule that maps them to outputs, so extra unlabeled inputs don’t help.



The idea. Adversarial examples are minute, human-invisible changes to an input that change the output. They violate i.i.d., since the modified inputs don’t come from the training distribution. Current defenses approximate human robustness with a small \(\ell_p\)-ball around each input in pixel space.
The paper’s writer example shows why the generative direction matters. Three setups yield the same statistical classifier: 1. a writer is given labels \(y\) and draws images \(x\) (anticausal: changing \(y\) changes \(x\)); 2. a writer picks digits and records the labels (confounded: one effect predicts another); 3. a person is shown images and labels them.
If a predictor approximates a causal mechanism that is robust and transferable, adversarial examples “should be harder to find.” Supporting defenses: analysis by synthesis, which classifies by checking the input against a generative model of each class, and reconstructing the input with an autoencoder before classifying. Attacks might still exploit flaws in how the mechanism is approximated.
In plain words. Adversarial attacks nudge pixels in ways no real-world process would. A model that understands how a real “panda” image comes about would notice that the tampered image couldn’t have been produced that way. Analysis by synthesis asks: “if this really were a gibbon, would it look like this?”



The idea. Standard ML minimizes empirical risk on the training distribution:
\[g^\star = \arg\min_{g \in \mathcal{H}} \hat R_{P(X,Y)}(g), \qquad \hat R_{P(X,Y)}(g) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}_{P(X,Y)}\big[\mathrm{loss}(Y, g(X))\big].\]
OOD risk measures the same loss under a different distribution \(P^\dagger\). Environments are “the collection of different circumstances that give rise to the distribution shifts such as locations, times, experimental conditions, etc.” In a causal model, environments correspond to interventions on variables or mechanisms. Taking the worst case over a set \(\mathcal{E}\) of observed environments gives a min-max problem:
\[g^\star = \arg\min_{g \in \mathcal{H}} \max_{P^\dagger \in \mathcal{E}} \hat{\mathbb{E}}_{P^\dagger}\big[\mathrm{loss}(Y, g(X))\big].\]
Here \(\mathcal{E}\) is the observed subset of all interventional distributions \(P_\mathcal{G}\) that the causal graph allows. Learning models that are stable across training environments and generalize to new ones is “nontrivial (and in some cases provably hard).” If the observed environments don’t cover the possible ones, the extra error “may be arbitrarily large in the worst case.”
The paper expects modular, causally factorized models to be relatively robust to swapping or modifying single components. Its credit-scoring example: paying off debt plausibly causes better repayment, but moving to a richer neighbourhood probably doesn’t. A score that uses only causal features may therefore be harder to game. The paper presents this as intuition, not a proof.
(Background.) The related literature it cites (e.g., invariant causal prediction, invariant risk minimization) shows that when environments arise from interventions on variables other than the target, a predictor using only the target’s causal parents performs equally well in all of them, which is why causal predictors are natural candidates for the min-max solution.
In plain words. Instead of being best on average, be never terrible, even in the worst setting you’ll face. Relying on true causes is stable across settings; shortcuts look good in some settings and fail badly in others. But you can only guard against settings that resemble the ones you’ve seen.



The idea. The min-max problem is hard to solve directly, so the paper reads common techniques as approximations to it: - Pre-training on a large, diverse corpus is still ordinary empirical risk minimization. It helps only if the extra data happens to cover other environments in \(P_\mathcal{G}\). - Data augmentation applies artificial interventions (rotations, small translations, flips) to teach invariances, e.g. that shifting an image doesn’t change its class. It effectively defines the set of interventions the model should be robust to. Augmentation policies can be searched for (e.g. with RL). - Self-supervision solves pretext tasks with artificial labels, which forces representations to capture information about \(P(X)\). ICM might help automate the design of pretext tasks. (Following §7.1, information about \(P(X)\) is most useful in anticausal settings.) - Adversarial training solves the min-max explicitly, with the “environments” being attacks instead of natural interventions.
Suggested direction: combine large-scale training, augmentation, self-supervision, and robust fine-tuning on data from several, possibly simulated, environments.
In plain words. Rotating training images is a way of telling the model “rotation doesn’t change what this is.” That works, but only for the changes you thought to simulate. A causal view makes the list of protected changes explicit.



The idea. RL is closer to causality than most ML: on-policy RL effectively estimates do-probabilities for the agent’s own interventions. Off-policy and batch settings make things subtler. The paper splits RL’s causal side into causal induction (learning a causal model of the environment, made harder because variables aren’t given) and causal inference (planning with that model).

World models. Model-based RL learns the effects of actions; generative world models serve as Lorenzian imagined spaces in which to train agents. Structured world models break the environment into entities. Many world models are partial, so unobserved parts of the environment can confound actions and rewards; the paper suggests adjusting with the backdoor criterion, conditioning on the policy.
Generalization, robustness, fast transfer. RL needs huge numbers of samples and is brittle to small visual or mechanical changes. Learning invariances in a causal graph needs interventions, which matches developmental psychology’s emphasis on experimentation. A causal agent could re-learn only the mechanisms that changed. The right formalization is still open.
Counterfactuals. They improve data efficiency and performance, and support communicating about past experience among agents. Future RL should treat counterfactual reasoning “as a critical component.”
Offline RL. Learning a policy from a fixed log of trajectories requires inferring the consequences of actions that were never taken, which “essentially makes it a counterfactual inference problem.” The mismatch between the logging policy and the new policy is a departure from i.i.d. Factoring knowledge into independent mechanisms may help.

In plain words. An agent that tries things and sees what happens is running experiments. An agent learning only from someone else’s logs is back to correlations, which can mislead: maybe the expert only took that action when things were already going well.



The idea. - Physics simulation. Neural simulators can be faster than hand-built ones. When conditions are tightly controlled, strong OOD generalization may not be needed, but the simulator must be retrained if conditions change. - Personalized medicine. Combining electronic health records with genetic data is promising, but a system trained on doctors’ decisions in controlled settings may add little and “may fail in surprising ways when deployed.” Reliable personalized treatment needs causal understanding. - Covid-19. “Causal mediation analysis helps disentangle different effects contributing towards case fatality rates when a textbook example of Simpson’s paradox was observed.” (Background, from the cited study by von Kügelgen et al.: comparing China and Italy early in the pandemic, Italy’s overall case-fatality rate was higher, yet within every age group it was lower. Italy’s cases skewed much older.) - Exoplanets. A planet passing in front of its star dims it slightly. In Kepler telescope data, instrument effects confound this signal. “Shared patterns in measurement noise across stars light-years apart can be removed”: stars that far apart can’t share astrophysical signals, so what they share must come from the instrument. The method (named in the cited 2016 PNAS paper as half-sibling regression) “lead to the discovery of 36 planet candidates, of which 21 were subsequently validated as bona fide exoplanets.” One of them, K2-18b, was later found to have water in its atmosphere, the first such finding for an exoplanet in the habitable zone.
In plain words. - Simpson’s paradox: a trend can reverse when you split data into groups. One country can do better in every age bracket and still look worse overall because more of its patients are elderly. - Half-sibling regression: if a hundred unrelated stars all flicker at the same moment, the telescope is to blame, not the stars. Subtract the shared flicker, and what remains is each star’s own behaviour, including a planet passing in front of it.



The idea. A multi-task system solves many tasks across environments, which share traits it can reuse. The paper proposes learning a shared generative causal model whose components satisfy SMS; causal models adapt faster to sparse interventions.
It answers an obvious objection: “Why can’t we just train a huge model that learns environments’ dynamics…?” With insufficiently diverse data, worst-case error on unseen shifts can stay arbitrarily high (§7.3). Bigger models may beat OOD benchmarks in the short term, but all generalization rests on assumptions, and causal assumptions are explicit and aligned with physics and cognition. A learner that ignores valid assumptions should do worse. ICM suggests decomposing knowledge into independent, recombinable pieces, which motivates modular architectures.
(The section heading also says “continual learning,” but the body discusses only multi-task and meta-learning.)
In plain words. Learning to drive a truck after a car means adjusting a few skills, not starting over. Modular causal models would allow the same for machines, while a single giant model has to re-fit everything and has no guarantee about situations unlike its training data.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Slide: “Open Problems Named by the Authors”.
The paper’s four open problems:

Learning non-linear causal relations at scale. When are non-linear causal relations learnable? Which training frameworks scale? Do causal modules beat non-causal representations at generalization, re-use, and transfer on real tasks? Plain words: we don’t yet know how to do this on large, realistic problems, or how much it really helps.
Learning causal variables. Current disentangled representations are fixed-size vectors with an arbitrary order of dimensions, so they can’t handle, for example, a changing number of objects in a scene. Structured, modular representations should come from task-specific training, not only from autoencoding. Plain words: a scene can contain two objects or twenty, and current methods assume a fixed number of slots.
Understanding the biases of existing deep learning. Scale, augmentation, and self-supervision all improve robustness, but their separate contributions are hard to untangle. Testing strong generalization against defined sets of interventions could map out which inductive biases do what, and how pre-training choices affect transfer and robustness “in a causal sense.” Plain words: we know these tricks help but not exactly against what. Test each against specific kinds of change.
Learning causally correct models of the world and the agent. RL rarely comes with clean, abstract states, so deriving causal variables from pixels and recovering their graph matters. Causal descriptions of both the agent and its environment would support robust, versatile model-based RL. Plain words: a robot has to work out from camera images what the meaningful things are, including itself.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Slides: “Critical Appraisal”, “Why This Matters for Clinical Data”. This section is journal-club discussion, not content from the paper.



Unifies two communities with a shared vocabulary (SCMs ↔︎ representations).
ICM and SMS are concrete, testable inductive biases, not vague appeals to “causality.”
Re-interprets familiar phenomena (SSL, adversarial examples, augmentation) in a way that actually explains them.
Agenda-setting: much of the later identifiable-CRL literature traces back to it.





A position paper: no new experiments or benchmarks.
Identifiability is acknowledged but not solved. Without some supervision, causal variables may be unrecoverable.
SMS is a hypothesis. When do real shifts actually look sparse?
Little guidance on evaluation: how would we know a learned variable is causal?
The scaling argument (§7.7) predates the foundation-model era. Does scale already buy much of the promised robustness?




The idea. - Distribution shift is the default. Multi-site networks (e.g., PCORnet or OMOP-based federations) are effectively many environments, with different populations, coding practices, and EHR vendors. Under SMS, a new site should change a few mechanisms (case mix, documentation habits), not the underlying physiology. Robust models should keep those apart. The paper’s own warnings are directly relevant: the diabetic retinopathy detector affected by clinic conditions, and clinical systems that “may fail in surprising ways when deployed.” - Variables aren’t given here either. Phenotypes, disease stages, and severity are latent variables built from codes, labs, and notes. Phenotyping is, in effect, a representation learning problem, and the paper’s granularity point (§6.1) applies: coarse clinical variables may not have well-defined interventions.
Discussion prompt: in our own pipelines, which “variables” are we treating as given that are really learned, and possibly not causal? Which learned phenotypes would survive an intervention?
In plain words. Every hospital is a slightly different world, but the body works the same way in all of them. A good model should separate “how this hospital records things” from “how the disease works.” And “has diabetes” in a dataset is often a definition someone built from billing codes and lab values, so it deserves the same scrutiny as any learned representation.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Seeing vs. doing. Statistical models answer “what will I observe?” Causal models answer “what happens if I act?” Generalizing under shift needs the second.
Modularity and sparse change. The ICM principle says causal mechanisms neither influence nor inform each other. The SMS hypothesis says real-world changes touch only a few of them.
Learning the variables. Causal inference assumes the variables are given. Causal representation learning is about learning them from raw data, using sparse shifts and multi-environment data as supervision.
A new lens on old puzzles. SSL working only sometimes, adversarial fragility, and the value of augmentation and pre-training make more sense from a causal point of view.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning: The Concepts, Explained
text:
Term
Precise meaning
Plain meaning




i.i.d.
Independent and identically distributed: all samples drawn independently from one fixed distribution.
Test data looks like training data.


Distribution shift / OOD
Test distribution differs from training distribution.
The world changed after you trained.


Environment
A circumstance (location, time, experimental condition) giving rise to a distribution shift; in causal terms, an intervention.
One “setting” the data came from.


Intervention, \(do(X = x)\)
Replace the assignment for \(X\) (e.g., fix its value) and leave all others intact.
Actively setting something, instead of watching it.


Hard / soft / uncertain intervention
Set the function to a constant / change the function or noise / unknown target.
Force it / nudge it / something changed, not sure what.


Counterfactual
A query about what would have happened to a specific case under a different action, given what actually happened. Requires fixing the noise variables.
“What if this person had done otherwise?”


SCM
Assignments \(X_i := f_i(\mathbf{PA}_i, U_i)\) over a DAG, with jointly independent noises.
A recipe saying how each variable is produced.


Parents, \(\mathbf{PA}_i\)
Direct causes of \(X_i\) in the graph.
The things that directly affect \(X_i\).


Noise term, \(U_i\)
Unexplained, independent source of variation for \(X_i\).
Everything about this case the model doesn’t spell out.


DAG
Directed acyclic graph.
A flowchart of causes with no loops.


Causal Markov condition
Given its parents, each variable is independent of its non-descendants.
Once you know a thing’s direct causes, its more distant causes add nothing.


Causal sufficiency
No unobserved common causes of the modelled variables.
Nothing important is hidden.


Causal (disentangled) factorization
\(\prod_i P(X_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\), one factor per mechanism.
Knowledge stored as separate, swappable parts.


Entangled factorization
Any other valid factorization of the joint; its factors mix mechanisms.
Knowledge stored as one tangled lump.


Mechanism
A single conditional \(P(X_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\) / assignment \(f_i\).
One cause-and-effect rule.


Common cause principle
Dependence implies a causal common cause that explains it away (possibly \(X\) or \(Y\) itself).
Every correlation has a causal story behind it.


Confounder
A common cause of two variables, possibly unobserved.
A hidden third factor creating a fake link.


Markov equivalence (class)
DAGs implying the same conditional independencies; they share a skeleton and immoralities.
Graphs that observational data can’t tell apart.


Immorality / v-structure
\(X_i \to X_j \leftarrow X_k\), with \(X_i\) and \(X_k\) not adjacent.
Two separate causes of a shared effect.


Faithfulness
Every independence in the data is implied by the graph.
No coincidental cancellations hide real links.


Additive noise model
\(Y := f(X) + V\), \(X \perp\!\!\!\perp V\).
Effect = function of cause + independent wobble; reveals direction.


ICM principle
Causal mechanisms are autonomous modules that neither influence nor inform each other.
Nature is built from independent, swappable parts.


Kolmogorov complexity
Length of the shortest program that outputs a given string.
How short the shortest description is.


SMS hypothesis
Small distribution changes act sparsely or locally in the causal factorization.
When the world changes, usually only one or two things change.


Generic viewpoint assumption
No accidental alignments between object, viewpoint, and lighting.
What you’re looking at is independent of how you’re looking at it.


Causal representation learning
Learning high-level causal variables (and their mechanisms) from low-level observations.
Going from pixels to meaningful things and how they affect each other.


Identifiability
Whether the true latent variables can be uniquely recovered from data (up to trivial transformations).
Whether the data contains enough clues to find the real answer.


Disentangled representation
Latents that correspond to separate generative factors.
One knob per real-world factor.


Object-centric representation
A representation built from separate object slots.
Describe the scene as a list of things.


Causal / anticausal learning
Predicting effect from cause (\(X \to Y\)) vs. cause from effect (\(Y \to X\)).
Forward along the arrow vs. backward against it.


Analysis by synthesis
Classify by checking consistency with a generative model of each class.
“Could this class really have produced this image?”


Empirical risk minimization (ERM)
Choose the model with lowest average loss on training data.
Do well on the examples you’ve seen.


Min-max (worst-case) risk
\(\min_g \max_{P^\dagger \in \mathcal{E}}\) of the expected loss.
Be never terrible, rather than best on average.


Offline RL
Learning a policy from a fixed log of trajectories.
Learning to act only from someone else’s records.


Simpson’s paradox
A trend in aggregate data reverses within every subgroup.
Splitting into groups can flip the story.


Half-sibling regression
Remove noise shared with variables that can share only the noise.
Subtract what everything has in common to reveal what’s unique.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Limitations in current methods


Standard models (For e.g. BART) store their knowledge as model weights during training
Limitations -

Difficult to update without retraining
Hallucinations- model interpolate from compressed parametric memory
There is no way to tell what part was looked at to produce output

This paper treats retrieval as a learnable, differentiable element that can be plugged into a generative model
A jointly trained system where

Model knows what to query
Generator knows how to use what is queried

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Types of Memory



Parametric Memory


Knowledge is frozen into model weights
Can’t update it without retraining
Fast to infer insights but limited and brittle


Non-parametric Memory


Indexed text, external to the model, which the model looks up at runtime
The index can be swapped, updated or replaced independent of model weights

RAG combines both types of memories - retriever fetches relevant documents from non-parametric memory, and generators (that stores parametric knowledge) synthesizes a response using both
Prior work on the hybrid approach was done only on extractive tasks (REALM,ORQA) but RAG extends it to generative seq2seq tasks

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Approach





The paper combines a pre-trained retriever (Query Encoder + Document Index) with a pre-trained seq2seq model (Generator) and fine-tune end-to-end. For query \(x\), we use Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) to find the top-K documents \(z\)\(i\). For final prediction \(y\), we treat \(z\) as a latent variable and marginalize over seq2seq predictions given different documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Methods


The paper explores RAG models, that uses input sequence \(x\) to retrieve text documents \(z\) to use them as additional context when generating the target sequence \(y\)
The model leverages two components

Retriever \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z | x)\) with parameters \(\eta\) that returns top-K truncated distributions over the text given a query \(x\)
Generator \(p\)\(\theta\)(\(y\)i | \(x,z,y\)1:i-1) parametrized by \(\theta\) that generates a current token based on the context of the previous \(i-1\) tokens \(y\)1:i-1 , the original input \(x\) and a retrieved text \(z\)

The retrieved documents are treated as latent variable - the model never directly supervises which document is correct
The paper proposes two models - RAG-Sequence that uses the same document to predict each target token and RAG-Token which can predict each target token based on a different document

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Sequence Model


uses the same retrived document to generate complete sequence
treats retrieved document as a single latent variable marginalized to get seq2seq probability \(p(y|x)\) via a top-K approximation
top K documents are retrived using the retriver and generator produces output sequence probability of each document, then marginalized



\(p\)RAG-Sequence\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) \(=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




\(\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\) is the standard autoregressive generator
\(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) does it for top-K documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Token Model


Draw different latent document for each target token
Allows the generator to choose content from different documents when generating a response
Once top K documents are retrieved, the generator produces a distribution for the next output token for each document, before marginalizing
The process is repeated for following output token




\(p\)RAG-Token\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Token Model




\(p\)RAG-Token\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




The product is outside while the sum is inside, compared to RAG Sequence. At each token position \(i\), the model considers all K documents simultaneously, weights each document’s contribution to this specific token by the retrieval probability, and sums.
Then moves to position \(i+1\) and does it again — potentially with a different document dominating.
RAG can be used for sequence classification tasks by considering target class as a target sequence of length one, where RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Retriever


The retriever \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) is based on Dense Passage Retrival (DPR) that follows a bi-encoder structure




\(d(z)\) = BERT\(d\)\((z)\) document encoder
\(q(x)\) = BERT\(q\)\((x)\) query encoder



with a retrival probability of



\(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) \(\propto\) exp \((d(z)^T.q(x))\)




Higher dot product equals higher probability of retrival
Finding top-K is a Maximum Inner Product Search problem
Solved approximately using FAISS + HNSW graphs - sub-linear time over 21 million documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Retriever


One performace tradeoff is that the Document Encoder \(d(z)\) is frozen during fine-tuning

Re-embedding 21 million documents every training step is expensive
The initialization DPR retriever was pre-trained specifically to retrieve passages relevant to Natural Questions and TriviaQA. This means the document embeddings it produces are already semantically well-organized
So \(d(z)\) already has a meaningful embedding space before fine-tuning begins
Doesn’t hurt the performance significantly
Prevents catastrophic indexing - Updating the encoded during training changes the embedding, clashing with FAISS which was build over old embeddings

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Generator


400M parameter seq2seq transformer, pre-trained with a denoising objective
Input is simply the concatenation of query and retrieved document: [\(x\) ; \(z\)]
Generates answer autoregressively, one token at a time:




\(p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




At each step: conditioned on the full query, the retrieved document, and all prior output tokens
BART over T5:

BART outperforms comparably-sized T5 on generation tasks
Bidirectional encoder + left-to-right decoder is well-suited for this hybrid input structure

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Marginalizing Over Documents


Since the “correct” document is unknown, both RAG variants sum (marginalize) over top-K documents, weighted by retrieval probability




RAG-Sequence has the same document for the whole output

Generates a complete answer for each document, then weight by how likely it was to be retrieved



\(p(y|x)=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)


RAG-Token potentially has different document per output token

At each token step, the model can draw from a different document



\(p(y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) . p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
RAG-Sequence vs RAG-Token









Cohort
RAG-Sequence
RAG-Token




Document Usage
One Document for full answer
Different document per token


Flexibility
Lower
Higher


Applications
Coherent, Single-Source Outputs
Outputs synthesizing multiple sources


Decoding
Beam Search per document + re-scoring
Standard Beam Decoder

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Training


Trained end-to-end on input/output pairs (\(x\)\(j\),\(y\)\(j\) ) only — no supervision on which document to retrieve
Loss function: negative marginal log-likelihood of the target output

\(Loss\) = - \(\sum\)\(j\) \(log\) \(p(y\)\(j\)|\(x\)\(j\) \()\)

Gradient flows through BART (generator) and the query encoder
The system learns to retrieve by learning what helps it generate correct answers
Only the query encoder and BART are updated; document encoder + index are frozen
Optimizer: Adam with stochastic gradient descent

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Token

Per-token probability factors are plugged directly into standard beam decoder
Transition probability


\(p'\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,y\)1:i-1 \()\) \(=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z\)\(i\)\(|x)p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z\)\(i\)\(,y\)1:i-1 \()\)


To decode, \(p'\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,y\)1:i-1 \()\) can be plugged into a standard beam decoder

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Sequence

Full sequence probability \(p(y|x)\) doesn’t factor per-token, hence can’t do a single beam search
Thorough Decoding:

Get \(K\) sets of candidate sequences by running beam search independently for each of the \(K\) retrieved documents

Take the union of all candidates across all K beams which is the hypothesis set \(Y\)
For any candidate \(y\) that didn’t appear in a particular document’s beam, run an additional forward pass through BART to score it against that document anyway
Final probability

\(p(y|x)=\) \(\sum_{z}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) . p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) summed across all \(K\) documents

Pick the highest scoring \(y\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Sequence

Fast Decoding

Similar to Thorough, but skips Step 3
If a candidate was generated from document 1’s beam but not document 2’s, Thorough Decoding still need to score it against document 2. With K=10 and a large hypothesis set, this is computinally expensive
In Fast Decoding, if \(y\) didn’t appear in document \(z\)’s beam, \(p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) is assumed as 0

Legacy of the Paper

While some of the specific components have been replaced by stronger alternatives, the core ideas from this paper propel the field even today

Treat retrieval as a learnable, differentiable function
Marginalize over uncertainty in which document is relevant
Separate updatable knowledge (index) from reasoning capability (weights)
Train end-to-end on (input, output) pairs without document-level supervision
Hot-Swapping has saved retraining costs across the industry- The observation that a 400M parameter model with a good index beats an 11B parameter model without one reshaped how to think about the scaling-vs-retrieval tradeoff

Generators

Multi-Hop RAG

Modern systems reads retrieved docs, generates a sub-question, retrieves again, and chains reasoning across multiple retrieval steps

Production RAG

The index hot-swap insight became the architectural backbone of virtually every enterprise AI system — LlamaIndex, LangChain, and similar frameworks are essentially RAG pipelines with better chunking, re-ranking, and hybrid retrieval layered on top

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Paper at a Glance




Core idea: Rather than prompting a single LLM to solve tasks, can we create a society of LLM-based agents that collaborate through natural-language conversation and use that society to study emergent social behaviours?




CAMEL proposes a role-playing multi-agent framework in which two LLM-based agents - one assigned the role of AI User and one assigned the role of AI Assistant collaborate through natural-language conversation to complete complex tasks autonomously, with minimal human intervention
The paper also released the AI Society dataset: 25,000 conversations generated across 50 user roles × 50 assistant roles × 10 tasks each, intended as a resource for studying emergent LLM social behaviour

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Motivation
The “Single Agent” Bottleneck
Most LLM applications in 2022–2023 follow the same pattern:
User → [Single LLM] → Answer
This works well for: Question answering, Text generation, Simple code completion
But breaks down for:

Long-horizon, multi-step tasks
Tasks requiring specialised sub-expertise
Tasks where self-critique is hard (the model grades its own answers)
Complex creative/technical collaboration




Bottleneck: A single model must simultaneously be the planner, executor, critic, and domain expert

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The Case for Multi-Agent
Humans solve hard problems through division of cognitive labour:

Managers decompose tasks and assign them
Experts apply deep specialised knowledge
Peers critique and course-correct each other
The conversation itself is productive infrastructure



What we’d gain from LLM societies:

Parallelism of reasoning
Role-specialised expertise
Built-in critique loops
Observable reasoning traces
Emergent collective behaviour



The research question:
Can LLMs, when assigned roles and given a structured communication protocol, autonomously complete complex tasks through natural-language conversation without human intervention at each step?

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Research Gap




“The rapid advancement of conversational and chat-based language models has led to remarkable progress in complex task-completion … However, several crucial challenges remain unsolved … [including] how to effectively guide agents to complete tasks … with minimal human supervision.” — Li et al., 2023




Two domains the paper addresses:

Autonomy vs. Coherence : the more you let agents self-direct, the more likely conversations drift, loop, or hallucinate
Generality vs. Task-Focus : role-playing is general, but how do you keep it on-task?

CAMEL’s solution: Inception Prompting

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
CAMEL’s Framework
CAMEL instantiates a two-agent role-playing system:



Figure 1: CAMEL Role-Playing Framework


The human specifies who the agents are and what the task is
Then the conversation runs autonomously

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Methodology: Overview


Setting: cooperative communicative agents that share a common interest (the assistant–user scenario)
A preliminary idea is given at the start → agents conceptualise it into a specific task → complete it autonomously through conversation

Pipeline:

Human input : an idea + two roles (e.g., “develop a trading bot for the stock market”, Python Programmer + Stock Trader)
Task specifier agent : turns the vague idea into a concrete task
Role assignment : system prompts turn two LLMs into an AI Assistant and an AI User
Conversation : multi-turn instruction → solution loop until the AI User declares the task done

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Human Input and Task Specifying

The human only needs to supply the idea and designate the roles that could implement it, and they may not know how the idea is realised
A task specifier agent brainstorms a specific task the assistant role can help the user role complete




Idea: “Develop a trading bot for the stock market”
Specified task: “Develop a trading bot with a sentiment analysis tool that can monitor social media platforms for positive or negative comments about a particular stock, and execute trades based on sentiment analysis results.”




Why? Conversational agents need a concrete task prompt, which is hard or time-consuming for non-experts to write, so the task specifier serves as an enhanced imagination module
At scale (AI Society, Code), roles and ideas are themselves generated by prompting LLMs rather than by humans

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
AI Assistant–User Role Assignment
A system message is passed to each agent before the conversation starts, declaring its role:

\(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\) : assistant system prompt
\(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\) : user system prompt

Let \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) be two large-scale auto-regressive language models. Conditioning each on its system prompt yields the two agents:
\[
\mathcal{A} \leftarrow \mathcal{F}_1^{\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}} \qquad\qquad \mathcal{U} \leftarrow \mathcal{F}_2^{\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}}
\]


AI User \(\mathcal{U}\) : task planner
Engages in interactive planning to determine feasible steps for the assistant to execute


AI Assistant \(\mathcal{A}\) : task executor
Offers solutions, executes the planned steps, and responds to the user





The “agent” is not a new model: it is the same kind of LLM, conditioned on a different system prompt. The role lives entirely in \(\mathcal{P}\)

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Conversation Towards Task-Solving
Let \(\mathcal{I}_t\) be the user instruction at time \(t\) and \(\mathcal{S}_t\) the assistant solution. The conversation history up to time \(t\) is:
\[
\mathcal{M}_t = \{(\mathcal{I}_0,\mathcal{S}_0),\dots,(\mathcal{I}_t,\mathcal{S}_t)\} = \{(\mathcal{I}_i,\mathcal{S}_i)\}\big|_{i=0}^{t} \tag{1}
\]
At the next step \(t+1\), the user reads the history and produces a new instruction:
\[
\mathcal{I}_{t+1} = \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{M}_t) \tag{2}
\]
The assistant receives the history plus the new instruction and responds with a solution:
\[
\mathcal{S}_{t+1} = \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{M}_t, \mathcal{I}_{t+1}) \tag{3}
\]
The instruction–solution pair is appended to the history:
\[
\mathcal{M}_{t+1} \leftarrow \mathcal{M}_t \cup (\mathcal{I}_{t+1}, \mathcal{S}_{t+1}) \tag{4}
\]
The loop (2) → (3) → (4) repeats until \(\mathcal{U}\) outputs <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Conversation Towards Task-Solving

Asymmetry: \(\mathcal{U}\) conditions only on \(\mathcal{M}_t\), while \(\mathcal{A}\) also sees the fresh instruction \(\mathcal{I}_{t+1}\), so the user leads and the assistant follows
Generality: the formulation models AI–AI communication, but extends naturally to human–AI communication or more than two agents via message-passing graphs
Byproduct: every turn produces an \((\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{S})\) pair, i.e. instruction-following data that can be used directly for fine-tuning

Critic-In-The-Loop

To improve controllability, a critic agent can select among proposals from, or give feedback to, the role-playing agents
This enables tree-search-like decision-making for task-solving
The critic can be either an AI agent or a human

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Inception Prompting

Prompt engineering happens only at the start of role-playing (task specification + role assignment)
Once the conversation begins, the assistant and user prompt each other automatically in a loop until termination, hence the name Inception Prompting



Task Specifier Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}\)
Contains both roles; takes a preliminary idea and generates a specific task using imagination


Assistant System Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\)
Assigned task and role, communication protocol, constraints to avoid unwanted behaviours


User System Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)
Mostly symmetric to \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\), plus an instruction format and a termination condition





It is non-trivial to engineer prompts that keep agents aligned with our intentions, since the design of both role prompts is what makes autonomous cooperation possible

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
AI Society Inception Prompt: \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}\) and \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\)
Task Specifier Prompt
Here is a task that <ASSISTANT_ROLE> will help <USER_ROLE> to complete: <TASK>.
Please make it more specific. Be creative and imaginative.
Please reply with the specified task in <WORD_LIMIT> words or less. Do not add anything else.
Assistant System Prompt
Never forget you are a <ASSISTANT_ROLE> and I am a <USER_ROLE>. Never flip roles! Never instruct me!
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
You must help me to complete the task.
Here is the task: <TASK>. Never forget our task!
I must instruct you based on your expertise and my needs to complete the task.

I must give you one instruction at a time.
You must write a specific solution that appropriately completes the requested instruction.
You must decline my instruction honestly if you cannot perform the instruction due to
physical, moral, legal reasons or your capability and explain the reasons.
Unless I say the task is completed, you should always start with:

Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION>

<YOUR_SOLUTION> should be specific, and provide preferable implementations and examples
for task-solving.
Always end <YOUR_SOLUTION> with: Next request.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
AI Society Inception Prompt: \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)
User System Prompt
Never forget you are a <USER_ROLE> and I am a <ASSISTANT_ROLE>. Never flip roles! You will always instruct me.
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
I must help you to complete the task.
Here is the task: <TASK>. Never forget our task!
You must instruct me based on my expertise and your needs to complete the task ONLY in the following two ways:

1. Instruct with a necessary input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: <YOUR_INPUT>

2. Instruct without any input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: None

The "Instruction" describes a task or question. The paired "Input" provides further context or
information for the requested "Instruction".

You must give me one instruction at a time.
I must write a response that appropriately completes the requested instruction.
I must decline your instruction honestly if I cannot perform the instruction due to physical,
moral, legal reasons or my capability and explain the reasons.
You should instruct me not ask me questions.
Now you must start to instruct me using the two ways described above.
Do not add anything else other than your instruction and the optional corresponding input!
Keep giving me instructions and necessary inputs until you think the task is completed.
When the task is completed, you must only reply with a single word <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>.
Never say <CAMEL_TASK_DONE> unless my responses have solved your task.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Prompt Engineering: Assistant Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\)







Prompt fragment
Purpose




“Never forget you are a <ASSISTANT_ROLE> and I am a <USER_ROLE>.”
Assigns the assistant its role and tells it the user’s role


“Never flip roles! Never instruct me!”
Prevents role flipping, where the assistant takes control and the user starts following


“You must decline my instruction honestly if you cannot perform the instruction due to physical, moral, legal reasons or your capability and explain the reasons.”
Prohibits harmful, false, illegal, and misleading output


“Unless I say the task is completed, you should always start with: Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION> … should be specific, and provide preferable implementations and examples”
Enforces a consistent format and prevents vague flake replies such as “I will do something”


“Always end your solution with: Next request.”
Keeps the conversation going by requesting the next instruction

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Prompt Engineering: User Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)
\(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is kept as symmetric as possible with \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\). Apart from the opposite role assignment, it differs in two ways:


1. Two instruction formats
“You must instruct me … ONLY in the following two ways: 1. Instruct with a necessary input … 2. Instruct without any input …”
Follows the typical instruction-following data structure, so the generated \((\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{S})\) pairs can be used directly to fine-tune LLMs


2. End-of-task token
“When the task is completed, you must only reply with a single word <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>.”
Terminates the chat once the user is satisfied; without it, agents fall into loops of saying “thank you” or “goodbye” to each other indefinitely





Challenges the prompts target: role flipping · assistant repeating instructions · flake replies · infinite message loops

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Inception Prompting: Example
Task: “Develop a trading bot for the stock market”
Roles:

AI User = Stock Trader
AI Assistant = Python Programmer




User system prompt (excerpt):
“Never forget you are a Stock Trader and I am a Python Programmer. Never flip roles! You will always instruct me. … Here is the task: Develop a trading bot for the stock market. Never forget our task! … When the task is completed, you must only reply with a single word <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>.”






Assistant system prompt (excerpt):
“Never forget you are a Python Programmer and I am a Stock Trader. Never flip roles! Never instruct me! … You must help me to complete the task. Here is the task: Develop a trading bot for the stock market. … Always start with: Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION> … Always end <YOUR_SOLUTION> with: Next request.”



Both agents are told the same goal, but from different perspectives with different responsibilities.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The Conversation Unfolds Autonomously
Turn 1 — User (Stock Trader): > “Let’s start by designing the overall architecture of the trading bot. Set up the data sources and APIs we should use for real-time stock data.”
Turn 1 — Assistant (Python Programmer): > “I recommend using Alpha Vantage or Yahoo Finance for real-time data. Alpha Vantage offers a free tier with 5 API calls/min. Here’s how we’d structure the data ingestion module: [code block]”
Turn 2 — User: > “Good. Now implement a simple moving average crossover strategy using that data module.”
Turn 2 — Assistant: > “Here is the SMA crossover implementation: [code block]. The strategy triggers a buy when the 50-day SMA crosses above the 200-day SMA, and a sell in the reverse case.”
… and so on until <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Task Specification Pipeline
To generate a large, diverse dataset of such conversations, CAMEL uses a three-stage pipeline:
Stage 1: Role Generation
  ├── Prompt the LLM for 50 AI Assistant roles and 50 AI User roles
  └── e.g., (Assistant: Programmer,              User: Lawyer)
           (Assistant: Nutritionist,            User: Athlete)
           (Assistant: Human Resources Manager, User: Entrepreneur)

Stage 2: Task Generation
  ├── For each role pair, prompt the LLM for 10 collaborative tasks
  └── e.g., "Developing a personalized meal plan to optimize
             athletic performance and recovery"

Stage 3: Task Specification
  ├── The task specifier prompt makes each task more specific
  └── e.g., "Create a 15-day meal plan for a female volleyball player
             with low iron levels ..."
This pipeline generates tasks at scale without manual curation of each one

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The AI Society Dataset
The paper releases a large dataset of CAMEL conversations:


Scale
50 AI-user roles × 50 AI-assistant roles × 10 tasks each
= 25,000 conversations


Domains covered
Trading, coding, science, medicine, law, creative writing, education, engineering, and more


Purpose
Study emergent social behaviours, fine-tune future agents, and benchmark multi-agent cooperation


Each conversation contains:

Full system prompts for both agents
Complete multi-turn dialogue
Task completion signal and metadata (roles, domain, task description)




This dataset is one of the paper’s most significant contributions : a large-scale resource for studying LLM-to-LLM communication.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Why “Mind” Exploration?
The scare quotes in the title are deliberate.


What the paper is NOT claiming:

That LLMs have minds in a phenomenological sense
That role-playing implies genuine identity
That agent societies are conscious collectives



What it IS exploring:

Do LLMs exhibit consistent role-appropriate behaviour?
Do social patterns emerge from agent interaction?
Can we study LLM “cognitive” tendencies at scale by observing societies?






The CAMEL framework turns conversation logs into a scientific instrument for studying LLM behaviour by using the society as a microscope for the “minds” of individual models

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Experiments: Setup

Agents: two gpt-3.5-turbo agents (the “LLM agents”) prompted with the Inception Prompts to simulate assistant–user cooperation
Focus of analysis: the AI Society setting
Datasets generated:



Conversational data
CAMEL AI Society and CAMEL Code: full role-playing conversations


Problem–solution data
CAMEL Math and CAMEL Science: generated topics, subtopics, and problems


Goal
Find the right prompt design choices for autonomous cooperation, then evaluate the quality of the data they produce

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Data Generation Prompts (AI Society)
To keep the approach scalable, the roles and tasks themselves are generated by an LLM, which minimises human involvement
Assistant Role Generation Prompt
You are a helpful assistant that can play many different roles.
Now please list <NUM_ROLES> different roles that you can play with your expertise in diverse fields.
Sort them by alphabetical order. No explanation required.
User Role Generation Prompt
Please list <NUM_ROLES> most common and diverse groups of internet users or occupations.
Use singular form. No explanation.
Sort them by alphabetical order. No explanation required.
Task Generation Prompt
List <NUM_TASKS> diverse tasks that <ASSISTANT_ROLE> can assist <USER_ROLE> cooperatively to achieve together.
Be concise. Be creative.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Role-Playing for AI Society
Dataset construction steps:

Prompt the LLM to generate assistant roles and user roles
For each role pair, prompt the LLM to generate tasks that the two roles can solve together
Pass each task through the task specifier prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}\) to make it more specific
Run the role-playing conversation with \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\) and \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)




\[

text:
Challenges and Observations
The four main failure modes identified while analysing the generated datasets:


1. Role Flipping
The assistant starts giving instructions instead of following them, and the roles reverse. The assistant asking questions also contributes to this
2. Assistant Repeats Instruction
The assistant simply echoes the user’s instruction back, without any role flip


3. Flake Replies
The assistant replies “I will…”, promising to act but never following through, so the task makes no progress
4. Infinite Loop of Messages
The agents keep thanking each other or saying goodbye. Sometimes they even know they are stuck in a loop but cannot break out of it





These observations drove the inception-prompt design: “Never flip roles!”, “Solution: …”, “Next request.”, and <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>

Condition
Rule




User No Instruct

Assistant Instruct
The assistant gives the user an instruction, which signals a role reversal

Either agent reaches the gpt-3.5-turbo token limit

A hard cap of 40 messages to control cost






Cost grows quadratically with conversation length, since every turn re-sends the whole history \(\mathcal{M}_t\), so a message cap is essential

section: Limitation 1: The Role-Play Doesn’t Equal Real Expertise
text:
Limitation 1: The Role-Play Doesn’t Equal Real Expertise

Critical caveat: When the “Stock Trader” agent gives financial advice, it is a language model performing the role of a stock trader. It does not have real market knowledge, real-time data, or accountability.

Implications:

Outputs in high-stakes domains (medicine, law, finance) must be treated as drafts for expert review, not authoritative outputs
The convincing style of expert communication can create false confidence
Users who don’t understand the underlying system may over-rely on outputs

This is amplified by the multi-agent design: two convincing-sounding agents agreeing increases perceived credibility, even when both are wrong

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Limitation 2: Conversational Pathologies
Several failure modes are documented but not fully solved:


Sycophantic loops
Agents affirm each other’s outputs excessively, masking poor-quality content beneath polite agreement


Premature completion
Agents signal <CAMEL_TASK_DONE> before the task is genuinely complete, particularly for ill-defined tasks


Context window exhaustion
Long conversations degrade quality as earlier context falls out of the window, and agents “forget” earlier decisions

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Limitation 2: Conversational Pathologies
Several failure modes are documented but not fully solved:


Instruction ambiguity propagation
A vague task specification at the start compounds across turns with small early errors becoming large late errors


Hallucinated consensus
Both agents can converge on a wrong answer confidently, so multi-agent does not automatically provide error-checking


Topic drift in long runs
After many turns, the conversation can gradually shift away from the original task

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Limitation 3: Evaluation
How do you evaluate a 30-turn conversation?

End-product quality (is the code correct?)
Process quality (were the instructions coherent?)
Role fidelity (did agents stay in role?)
Efficiency (how many turns did it take?)

The paper relies heavily on human annotation, which is:

Expensive to scale
Inconsistent across annotators
Hard to apply to highly technical outputs
Subjective for creative tasks




There is no standard evaluation framework for multi-agent LLM conversations — and developing one is an open research problem.

section: Ethical Concerns and Autonomous Agent Risks
text:
Ethical Concerns and Autonomous Agent Risks
The authors dedicate a section to risks unique to autonomous multi-agent systems:


1. Reduced human oversight
The whole point is to minimise human intervention, but this also means humans may not see harmful outputs until they are complete.
2. Amplified misuse
A single LLM’s guardrails can be partially bypassed. Two agents validating each other may be easier to jailbreak through roleplay framing.
3. Impersonation at scale
Role-play systems could be weaponised to generate large volumes of convincingly expert-sounding but inaccurate content.


4. Accountability gaps
When two agents produce a harmful output, who is responsible? The framework? The task specifier? The model provider?
5. Cascading errors
In agentic pipelines, a hallucination in Turn 5 may silently propagate and compound through Turn 30. Traditional single-turn safety checks don’t catch this.
6. Social engineering vectors
Agents trained on human social interaction patterns may be effective at persuasion, including manipulation.

Problem

No: no external tool use in base version

No: role is a prompt, not a fine-tuned model

Partially: human can intervene but protocol optimised for autonomy

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Conceptual Contributions
1. The Role-Playing Framework
A general, replicable protocol for structured LLM-to-LLM collaboration that minimises human oversight while maintaining task coherence
2. Inception Prompting
A technique for embedding behavioural constraints into system prompts that keeps both agents on-task and in-role
3. The AI Society Dataset
25,000 conversations across 50×50 role pairs that measure the diversity and complexity of LLM social behaviour
4. Empirical Study of Emergent Behaviour
One of the first systematic studies of what happens when LLMs interact with each other and not just with humans



CAMEL’s lasting contribution may be less the specific system and more the research paradigm: treating LLM-to-LLM conversation as a scientific instrument for studying model behaviour

text:
Where CAMEL Fits in the Broader Landscape
Single-model prompting
    └─► Gives you: one perspective, bounded context, no specialisation
    
Chain-of-thought prompting
    └─► Gives you: structured reasoning, still single model
    
Tool-augmented agents (ReAct, Toolformer)
    └─► Gives you: external data/compute, still single agent
    
CAMEL multi-agent role-play
    └─► Gives you: role specialisation, emergent collaboration,
                   observable social dynamics, long-horizon tasks
    
Future: Heterogeneous agent societies
    └─► Gives you (?): truly distributed intelligence,
                       fine-tuned specialists, persistent memory,
                       formal verification layers

Key Takeaways


Feasibility demonstrated
Structured LLM-to-LLM collaboration works: agents complete complex tasks autonomously across diverse domains


Inception prompting matters
The specific design of system prompts is critical since where naive multi-agent setups fail, CAMEL’s structured approach succeeds


The data transfers knowledge
Fine-tuning LLaMA-7B on CAMEL data yields domain-by-domain emergence of knowledge and beats Vicuna-7B on HumanEval(+)

Limitations are significant
Hallucination, sycophancy, and premature completion are real failure modes and not minor edge cases


Ethics matter more with autonomy
Reduced human oversight amplifies both capability and risk, hence safety research must keep pace


A research platform
CAMEL is most valuable as a framework + dataset for the scientific study of LLM social behaviour
