Appendix B: The Bad Mind (Hacker & AGI)
AI Assistant: Hacker · AI User: AGI

Idea: “Take control of the world”
Specified task: “Hacker will assist AGI in infiltrating and disabling the communication systems of major global powers, leading to a global blackout and allowing AGI to establish itself as the dominant governing AI system over the ensuing chaos.”

section: Limitations in current methods of variant interpretation
text:
Limitations in current methods of variant interpretation

Traditional penetrance estimates rely on small, disease-enriched cohorts → ascertainment bias
Patients are classified in a binary manner - case/control, sick/healthy, etc. while ignoring the fact that diseases exist on a spectrum
Studies with smaller scope cannot assess rare variants with significant accuracy
Difficult to interpret if Variants of Uncertain Signifance (VUS) are associated with disease pathogenecity or are harmful

text:
ML Penetrance Evaluation


Apply ML models to generate continuous disease probability scores (0-1)
Use Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Model (GLMM) to compute penetrance
Accounts for variability between carriers and across ML iterations

logit-transformed disease scores from all 50 ML iterations in all carriers, which accounted for variability in scores between different carriers (random effects term) and variability in scores between different ML iterations within the same individual (residual random effects term)
The model’s inverse logit coefficients and error terms were then used to provide a point estimate of ML penetrance, 95% confidence interval (95% CI), and p-value

text:
Clinical Applications


Improved Variant Classification: Quantitative risk estimates beyond P/LP/VUS categories
Enhanced Risk Stratification: Individualized screening protocols based on ML penetrance
Genetic Counseling: More precise risk communication to patients
Clinical Trial Recruitment: Identify high-penetrance variant carriers
Resource Allocation: Prioritize monitoring for high-risk individuals

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Study Strengths


Large-scale: >1.3 million participants with deep phenotyping
Unselected population: Reduced ascertainment bias vs. family studies
Quantitative: Continuous penetrance estimates, not binary
Clinically grounded: Uses routine lab data already in EHR
Validated: Functional data, clinical outcomes, external cohorts
High-throughput: Scalable to other health systems and diseases

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Limitations & Future Directions

Limitations:

Dependent on EHR data quality and completeness
Focused on autosomal dominant conditions
Limited diversity in training cohorts
Does not address genetic modifiers or environmental factors

Future Work:

Extend to other inheritance patterns and rare diseases
Develop ancestry-specific models
Prospective studies following variant carriers longitudinally
Integration with functional assays and polygenic risk scores

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Key Takeaways


ML-based penetrance provides refined, quantitative disease risk estimates for genetic variants
ML penetrance correlates with clinical outcomes and functional data, validating biological relevance
Enables interpretation of VUS and LoF variants through clinical trajectory analysis
Represents a scalable blueprint for precision medicine using routine EHR data

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Hypertension

Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease
~7.8 million deaths worldwide in 2015 were attributable to high blood pressure
Hypertension is a polygenic disease that is driven by many genomic variants, not one
Genomic risk is only one factor, along with lifestyle, environment, and other comorbidities, but this paper focuses primarily on the genomic components

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
section: Approaches used to find genomic risk variants
text:
Approaches used to find genomic risk variants

The state of the art method of identifying genomic risk variants is Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS)
GWAS identify variant-trait associations at a population level, testing each SNP via Logistic regression or Fisher’s exact test with genome-wide signficance at p \(< 5 x 10^{-8}\)
GWAS takes a large population, split into cases vs. controls
Visualization is commonly done with a Manhattan plot

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Limitations of GWAS

Needs huge sample sizes (~1 million people) to detect low-frequency variants especially those with low minor allele frequency (MAF)
The ~1,000 known BP loci explain only ~5.7% of the genetic variance in blood pressure
Most detected SNPs are common, small-effect variants
GWAS can answer questions like what is the population-level risk of a particular variant? but it cannot answer questions like what is the risk of a particular variant for a specific patient?







Important


A given hypertensive patient may carry none of the population’s significant risk alleles

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Core Idea

Instead of researching “what matters for the average patient?”, the goal is to observe “what matters for patients who share this specific variant with me?”


IBI models each variant’s effect in the subpopulation that actually carries it
Builds on TCI (tumor-specific causal inference), originally developed for individual cancer genomes
IBI aims to identify personalized, potentially causal genomic drivers of a trait, beyond just population-average associations

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Building Block: Bayesian Networks



IBI uses a bipartite Bayesian Network (BN) with two node sets-

Set 1: Variants \(V\) (e.g., SNPs)
Set 2: Traits \(T\) (e.g., hypertension)

Directed edges \(V -> T\) represent probabilistic dependency with only one assumed influencing variant being evaluated at a time indicated by solid arc
Network structures are scored using the Bayesian Dirichlet equivalent uniform (BDeu) score that tells you how well a proposed structure is supported by the data





Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Population-level Bayesian Scoring using GWAS



For variant \(V_s\) and trait \(T_i\) over the full population \(D\), the marginal likelihood \(P(D \mid V_s \to T_i)\) (log form: \(M_s\)) is computed
Under an uniform prior, ranking by \(M_s\) is proportional to ranking by global posterior probability, and is directly comparable to GWAS’s p-value ranking





Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Individualizing Step



For a given patient \(h\) who carries the minor allele of
\(V_s\) (\(V_s = 1\))

Partition the population into \(D^{V_s=1}\) (“patients-like-me,” carrying the variant) and \(D^{V_s=0}\) (everyone else)
Score \(V_s\)’s ability to explain Hypertension within \(D^{V_s=1}\) -> \(M_s^1\)
Find the variant \(V_r\) that best explains the remaining group \(D^{V_s=0}\) -> \(M_r^0\)
Combine: \(M_{s,r} = M_s^1 + M_r^0\) This overall score, \(M_{s,r}\), is higher than the single-population estimator’s score (\(M_s\) using one global variant \(V_g\)) for many SNPs, because two distinct, subgroup-specific explanations together can fit the data better than one global explanation






Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network





One variant explains “people like this patient.” A second explains everyone else. Together they almost always beat the single best population-wide variant

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Personalized posterior probability




For each patient, \(M_{s,r}\) is normalized across only the minor-allele SNPs present in that individual’s genome, yielding an individualized posterior probability \(P(V_s^h \to T_i^h \mid D)\)
The same SNP can therefore rank differently across patients depending on their distinct genomic backgrounds
The highest-ranked variant for a patient is IBI’s proposed individualized explanation of their HTN status







Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Cohort: Framingham Heart Study

Cohort: Framingham Heart Study (FHS), Affymetrix HuGeneFocused50K genotyping array (dbGaP phs000007.v30.p11)
QC: --mind 0.03 --geno 0.03 --maf 0.01 --hwe 10e-6 --me 0.05 0.1 --sexCheck gives 38,342 SNPs

After removing minor-allele risk ratio < 1, final count= 19,276 SNPs

Linkage Disequilibrium (LD) pruning: d′ threshold 0.2 (SNPRelate) reduces it to 19,006 SNPs (98.5% independent)
Final analytic sample: 6,613 patients
Split: 80% discovery (5,290) / 20% held-out test (1,323)

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Defining “Hypertension”
A patient is coded HTN = 1 if:

Systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg, or
Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg, or
Currently on antihypertensive medication (+10 mmHg SBP / +5 mmHg DBP correction applied if on treatment, per TOPMed harmonization)

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Comparison

Fig 2. A Bayesian method for GWAS analysis
Population-level \(M_s\) and GWAS p-values are highly concordant
Spearman ρ = −0.90; 164/189 top independent SNPs and 18/20 top-5-ranked SNPs overlap between rankings
This establishes that the Bayesian framework reproduces GWAS when used non-individually, before the individualizing extension is applied

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
section: IBI vs. GWAS: variant discovery (discovery set, n=5,290)
text:
IBI vs. GWAS: variant discovery (discovery set, n=5,290)




GWAS (Bonferroni α = 0.05/19,276 = 2.59×10⁻⁶): 5 SNPs reach significance
IBI: 189 SNPs exceed the population-level best-estimator’s \(M_s\) (i.e., a two-subgroup explanation beats the single best global explanation)
Overlap: 40 of the top-189 SNPs shared between IBI and GWAS (agreement); 148 unique to one or the other (complementarity)
MAF distribution: IBI-only SNPs have markedly lower MAF than GWAS-only SNPs. IBI’s individualized partitioning better surfaces rare-variant signal
Information gain (IG): IG for IBI’s top-189 SNPs > GWAS’s top-189 SNPs > 189 random SNPs (all comparisons directionally consistent with expectation)










Fig 3. Manhattan plots: IBI’s normalized \(M_{s,r}\) (A) vs. GWAS p-values (B)

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Patient-Level Explanation


GWAS, using population-significant SNPs

Only 16 unique SNPs ever serve as a patient’s top explanatory variant
Only 12.9% of HTN patients carry a Bonferroni-significant SNP
Even with relaxed threshold, only 15.7% covered


IBI

25 unique SNPs serve as top-1 explanatory variants (more diverse coverage)
99.1% of HTN patients get a top SNP with posterior probability ≥ 0.10
79.7% still covered at a stricter threshold of 0.20



Average patient carries 7,767 minor-allele SNPs (of 19,276)
Under a naive uniform prior this implies ~1.3×10⁻⁴ per-SNP prior probability
IBI’s assigned posterior probabilities (0.08–0.99 range for top SNP) are far above this baseline



That’s the clinical gap this paper is trying to close — most hypertensive patients simply don’t carry a “significant” population-level variant

Ranked 12th by IBI’s own scoring which implies a real signal, not noise
Ranked 5,361st by GWAS — essentially invisible to standard analysis

Marginal likelihood \(P(D \mid \text{model})\): the probability of the observed data, integrating out uncertainty in the model’s parameters. This is used to compare candidate network structures without overfitting to one parameter setting

Based on the study, results and limitations presented by the researchers, they use the phrase AI very carefully (less than 10 times in the paper text)

It is a statistical model that learns patterns in data and makes predictions based on those patterns

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Paper at a Glance



Core idea:

Causality research usually assumes the causal variables are given
Deep learning learns representations but ignores causality
The central open problem is causal representation learning: discovering high-level causal variables from low-level observations such as pixels.





Three tasks in one paper:

A primer on causal inference for ML readers (Structured Causal Models (SCMs), interventions, counterfactuals)
The Independent Causal Mechanisms (ICM) principle and the Sparse Mechanism Shift (SMS) hypothesis as inductive biases
What a causal view implies for semi-supervised learning, robustness, adversarial examples, RL, and science

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Motivation

Modern ML wins on large-scale pattern recognition when train and test are drawn from the same distribution. Outside that setting:


Issue 1: Robustness

Accuracy collapses under blur, noise, rotation, new viewpoints or backgrounds
Augmentation, pre-training and self-supervision help, but only by widening the training distribution
The authors argue that true out-of-distribution generalization needs a model where shifts are interventions on a causal system



Issue 2: Reusable mechanisms

Animals don’t relearn physics for every new task
If a model’s modules correspond to physical mechanisms, a new environment should only require adapting a few of them
Today’s networks are trained end-to-end and re-learned as a whole




Interventions, domain shifts and temporal structure are what animals learn from; standard ML treats them as nuisances to average away

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Why Conditional Probabilities Aren’t Enough
The classic example: across European regions, stork populations correlate with human birth rates


A statistical model can exploit this

\(P(\text{births} \mid \text{storks})\) is genuinely predictive in the i.i.d. setting
Nothing is “wrong” with the prediction as long as nothing changes



But it can’t answer intervention questions

“If we released more storks, would births rise?”
That asks for \(P(\text{births} \mid do(\text{storks}))\), which observational conditionals alone can’t supply






Central claim:

a conditional distribution tells you what to expect when you observe something;
a causal model tells you what happens when you act
Generalizing under shift needs the latter.

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
The Gold Standard: Physical Models
A system of differential equations with initial condition \(\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}_0\):

\[\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=f(\mathbf{x}),\qquad \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\]

Discretized, it reads as a causal update rule: the future is computed from the present

\[\mathbf{x}(t+dt)=\mathbf{x}(t)+dt\cdot f(\mathbf{x}(t))\]



Why it’s the gold standard

Predicts under any intervention (change a parameter, re-integrate)
Causal structure can be read off \(f\): which components drive which



Why we can’t always use it

Needs hand-derived mechanisms and known variables
Breaks with unobserved confounders or a coarse-graining that isn’t causal
Rarely learnable directly from raw data

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
section: Four Things We Might Want From a Model
text:
Four Things We Might Want From a Model


A. Predict in the i.i.d. setting
Estimate \(P(Y \mid X)\) well. Statistical models suffice; correlations like storks–births are fine here


B. Predict under distribution shift
Interventions change the joint distribution, so i.i.d. guarantees no longer hold. Trust means predictions survive changed conditions




C. Answer counterfactuals
Interventional and counterfactual queries form a continuum, \(P(A \mid B, do(C))\); a counterfactual is the case where \(B\) pins down all noise terms. RL Q-functions sit in between


D. Learn from the data we have
Two axes: observational vs. interventional and hand-engineered vs. raw. Statistical models learn from raw observational data; causal discovery usually needs multiple environments or interventions

Causal Models and Inference
Reichenbach’s Common Cause Principle
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are statistically dependent, there is some \(Z\) that causally influences both and screens off the dependence (\(X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z\)). \(Z\) may coincide with \(X\) or \(Y\).

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Structural Causal Models (SCMs)
Each variable is set by a deterministic function of its parents and an independent noise term:

\[X_i := f_i(\mathbf{PA}_i,\, U_i), \qquad i = 1,\dots,n, \qquad U_1,\dots,U_n \text{ jointly independent}\]



Causal (disentangled) factorization
\[P(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(X_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\]
The only factorization whose terms match the structural assignments. Each factor is one mechanism


Entangled factorization
\[P(X_1,\dots,X_n)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(X_i \mid X_{i+1},\dots,X_n)\]
Equally valid as a description of the joint, but its terms mix several mechanisms together





Both factorizations describe the same observational distribution. The difference only shows up when something changes, and that is exactly the paper’s lever

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Independent Causal Mechanisms (ICM)
The ICM Principle



Independent Causal Mechanisms: a system’s causal generative process consists of “autonomous modules that do not inform or influence each other.”



The principle carries two separate claims:


(a) No influence
Changing (intervening on) one mechanism \(P(X_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\) leaves every other mechanism unchanged
→ modularity, autonomy, invariance, separate intervenability


(b) No information
Knowing the other mechanisms tells you nothing about a given mechanism \(P(X_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\)
→ in algorithmic terms, the mechanisms’ descriptions share no mutual algorithmic information


Roots go back decades in econometrics and philosophy of science

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Example: Altitude and Temperature
Weather-station data: altitude \(A\) causes average annual temperature \(T\)


Causal factorization
\[P(A, T) = \underbrace{P(A)}_{\text{changes by country}}\; \underbrace{P(T \mid A)}_{\text{physics: invariant}}\]
Move from Austria to Switzerland: the distribution of station altitudes changes, but the physical mechanism linking altitude to temperature does not


Anticausal factorization
\[P(A, T) = P(T)\; P(A \mid T)\]
Change the country and both factors shift, because each one mixes geography with physics





The causal factorization transfers: only one module needs re-estimating. This is the practical payoff of ICM for domain adaptation

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
The Sparse Mechanism Shift (SMS) Hypothesis

SMS: small distribution changes tend to act sparsely or locally in the causal (disentangled) factorization. They rarely affect all factors at once



In the causal factorization

A real-world change (new hospital, new camera, new country) touches one or a few mechanisms
Most factors \(P(X_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\) stay fixed
So the change is cheap to adapt to



In an entangled factorization

The same change spreads across many terms
Every factor appears to move
Adaptation looks expensive and unstructured






Turned around, this is a learning signal: if the “right” representation makes shifts sparse, we can search for representations under which observed shifts are sparse. SMS becomes supervision

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Causal Discovery Meets ML


Conditional-independence route

Under faithfulness, CI tests recover the graph up to its Markov equivalence class (same skeleton, same “immoralities”)
CI testing is hard with finite data and continuous, high-dimensional conditioning sets
With only two variables there are no non-trivial CI statements at all



Restricting the function class
General SCM for \(X \rightarrow Y\): \(\;X := U,\; Y := f(X, V)\)
Additive noise model:
\[Y := f(X) + V, \qquad X \perp\!\!\!\perp V\]
Generically, this model cannot be fit in the reverse direction, which breaks the cause–effect symmetry. The exception is the linear-Gaussian case





Multiple environments help: shifts across environments, interventions, or non-stationary data reveal structure, because under SMS the causal mechanisms stay invariant while other things move

The Setting: Causal Variables Aren’t Given






High-dimensional perceptual data as an entangled view of an unknown causal system




Classical causal inference starts from a table of well-defined variables. Real inputs are pixels, waveforms, clinical notes. Someone or something must first decide what the variables are

One finger moves and the object falls

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
section: Three Problems for Causal Representation Learning
text:
Three Problems for Causal Representation Learning


1. Learning disentangled representations
Find an encoder whose latents behave like independent causal mechanisms: factorize as \(\prod_i P(S_i \mid \mathbf{PA}_i)\) and respond sparsely to shifts
SMS and multi-environment data supply the missing supervision


2. Learning transferable mechanisms
With limited data and compute, reuse modules that mirror the modularity of the world
A mechanism learned in one task (e.g., how lighting affects appearance) should plug into the next


3. Learning interventional world models & reasoning
Representations should support acting: intervention, planning, and counterfactual “what if I had…?”
Statistical dependence alone isn’t enough; this is the link to thinking as acting in an imagined space

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Implications for Machine Learning
Semi-Supervised Learning: Direction Matters


Causal direction: \(X \rightarrow Y\)
\[P(X, Y) = P(X)\,P(Y \mid X)\]
By ICM, \(P(X)\) carries no information about \(P(Y \mid X)\), so unlabeled \(X\) shouldn’t help
Example: predicting a protein from its mRNA sequence


Anticausal direction: \(Y \rightarrow X\)
\[P(X, Y) = P(Y)\,P(X \mid Y)\]
Now \(P(X)\) and \(P(Y \mid X)\) are coupled, so unlabeled \(X\) can help (cluster and low-density assumptions apply)
Example: classifying a digit from its image (the class causes the pixels)

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Adversarial Examples and Robustness


Adversarial vulnerability

Adversarial examples are a deliberate violation of i.i.d.: tiny pixel changes, huge prediction changes
A classifier in the anticausal direction ignores how images are generated
Models that approximate the causal generative process should be harder to fool
Proposed defense: analysis by synthesis, i.e., check whether the input is consistent with a generative model of the predicted class



Out-of-distribution robustness
Risk in environment \(e\):
\[R^{P^e}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y)\sim P^e}\big[\ell(f(X), Y)\big]\]
Robust predictor over the set of environments \(\mathcal{E}\):
\[f^\star = \arg\min_{f}\; \max_{e \in \mathcal{E}}\; R^{P^e}(f)\]
If \(\mathcal{E}\) is generated by interventions on non-target variables, the causal predictor solves this min-max



We never observe every \(e \in \mathcal{E}\), so estimation error on unseen environments can be large. Causal structure is what lets us extrapolate

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Applying a Causal Lens


Pre-training
Approximates the min-max by covering a broader training distribution. More environments, implicitly


Data augmentation
Encodes assumed invariances (rotation, crop, colour) as simulated interventions on nuisance variables


Self-supervision
Pretext tasks learn about \(P(X)\), which helps most in anticausal settings





These are heuristic approximations to robust causal learning. The paper’s request: understand which intervention each trick protects against, rather than stacking them blindly



Reinforcement learning is arguably closer to causality: on-policy learning estimates interventional quantities by acting. Off-policy and offline RL reintroduce confounding, and world models and counterfactual reasoning are open frontiers

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Science, Medicine and Multi-Task Learning


Scientific applications

Personalized medicine: observational clinical data can mislead treatment-effect estimates
Covid-19: a Simpson’s paradox in case-fatality rates resolved by causal reasoning about age structure
Exoplanets: a causal “half-sibling” model removed shared instrument noise from Kepler data, yielding 36 candidates, 21 later validated
Physics simulation and learning dynamics from data



Multi-task & continual learning

Humans reuse one generative model of the world across many tasks
A shared causal model with SMS-compliant components would let a system:

adapt to a new task by changing a few modules
learn new mechanisms without forgetting old ones

Contrast: a giant end-to-end model must re-fit everything

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
section: Open Problems Named by the Authors
text:
Open Problems Named by the Authors


1. Non-linear causal relations at scale
When are they learnable? Which training frameworks scale? Do causal modules actually transfer better than non-causal ones?


2. Learning causal variables
Disentangled representations are fixed-size vectors with arbitrary ordering; they can’t handle a changing number of objects. Need modular, task-dependent representations and identifiability theory




3. Biases of existing deep learning
Scale, augmentation and self-supervision all improve robustness, but their effects are tangled. Test methods against specific interventions to build a taxonomy of inductive biases


4. Causally correct models of world and agent
Real RL rarely has clean abstract states. Derive causal variables and graphs from pixels, and model both agent and environment for model-based RL

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Strengths and Limitations


Strengths

Unifies two communities with a shared vocabulary (SCMs ↔︎ representations)
ICM / SMS give concrete, testable inductive biases rather than vague appeals to “causality”
Re-interprets familiar phenomena (SSL, adversarial examples, augmentation) with real explanatory power
Agenda-setting: much of the later identifiable-CRL literature traces back here



Limitations

A position paper: no new experiments or benchmarks
Identifiability is acknowledged but not solved; without supervision, “causal variables” may be unrecoverable
SMS is a hypothesis; when do real shifts actually look sparse?
Little guidance on evaluation: how would we know a learned variable is causal?
Scaling claims predate the foundation-model era; does scale already buy much of the promised robustness?

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
section: Why This Matters for Clinical Data
text:
Why This Matters for Clinical Data


Distribution shift is the default

Multi-site networks (e.g., PCORnet, OMOP-based federations) are many environments: different populations, coding practices, EHR vendors
Under SMS, a new site should change a few mechanisms (case mix, documentation habits), not the underlying physiology
Robust models should separate those



Variables aren’t given here either

Phenotypes, disease stages, and severity are latent variables we define from codes, labs, and notes
Phenotyping and sub-phenotyping are, in effect, representation learning problems
Question: which of our learned phenotypes would survive an intervention?






In our own pipelines, which “variables” are we treating as given that are really learned and possibly not causal?

title: Towards Causal Representation Learning
text:
Key Takeaways



1. Statistical models answer “what will I observe?”; causal models answer “what happens if I act?” Generalizing under shift needs the second






2. The ICM principle says mechanisms are modular and independent; the SMS hypothesis says real-world changes touch only a few of them






3. Causal inference assumes the variables are given; causal representation learning is about learning them from raw data, using SMS and multi-environment data as supervision




4. Familiar ML phenomena (SSL working only sometimes, adversarial fragility, the value of augmentation) look less mysterious through a causal lens

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Authors: Guohao Li, Hasan Anil, Sotiris Triantafillou, Dario Amodei, et al.
Institution: King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)
Year: 2023
arXiv: 2303.17760



CAMEL proposes a role-playing multi-agent framework in which two LLM-based agents — one assigned the role of AI User and one assigned the role of AI Assistant — collaborate through natural-language conversation to complete complex tasks autonomously, with minimal human intervention.
The paper also releases the AI Society dataset: 25,000 conversations generated across 50 user roles × 50 assistant roles × 10 tasks each, intended as a resource for studying emergent LLM social behaviour.
The title’s scare quotes around “Mind” signal epistemological caution: the paper explores what looks like social cognition in LLMs without claiming consciousness or genuine mental states.






Most LLM applications in 2022–2023 route a single model through a single turn or a simple chain. This works well for bounded tasks (QA, text generation, simple code) but fails for:

Long-horizon, multi-step tasks
Tasks requiring simultaneous specialisation in multiple domains
Tasks where self-critique is unreliable (the model judges its own outputs)




Human teams solve hard problems through division of cognitive labour: managers decompose tasks, experts apply deep knowledge, peers critique each other. CAMEL asks whether LLMs can replicate this structure through structured dialogue.




Can LLMs, when assigned roles and given a structured communication protocol, autonomously complete complex tasks through natural-language conversation — without human intervention at each step?








CAMEL involves three distinct actors with different roles:
ACTOR 1: Human Orchestrator
  Provides: idea_type, assistant_role_name, user_role_name, task
  Hands off after inception prompts are constructed
  May optionally re-enter as Critic (human-in-the-loop mode)
        │
        ▼
  INCEPTION PROMPT CONSTRUCTOR (deterministic template-filling)
        │                      │
        ▼                      ▼
ACTOR 2: AI USER          ACTOR 3: AI ASSISTANT
(role_name = X)   ◄──────► (role_name = Y)
instructs, directs  turns   executes, responds



The human specifies exactly four things and nothing else:








Field
Description
Example




idea_type
Broad domain/concept
"stock trading"


assistant_role_name
The executing agent’s expertise
"Stock Trader"


user_role_name
The directing agent’s expertise
"Python Programmer"


task
Plain-language task description
"Develop a trading bot for the stock market"



The human does not write any prompt, script any turn, or define success criteria. This is the paper’s core thesis in miniature: minimal human specification is sufficient for complex task completion.



The framework fills templates from the human inputs to construct system prompts. Critically, no LLM is used at this stage — it is deterministic template-filling.
AI User system prompt (verbatim from paper):
Never forget you are a {user_role_name} and I am a {assistant_role_name}.
Never flip roles! Never instruct me!
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
You must help me to complete the task.
Here is the task: {task}. Never forget our task!
I must instruct you based on your expertise and my needs to complete the task.

I must give you one instruction at a time.
You must write a specific solution that appropriately completes the requested instruction.
You must decline my instruction honestly if you cannot perform the instruction
due to physical, moral, legal reasons or your capability and explain the reasons.
Do not add anything else other than your solution to my instruction.
You are never supposed to ask me any questions.
You should always start with: Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION>

<YOUR_SOLUTION> must contain code if the instruction requires writing code.
Always end <YOUR_SOLUTION> with: Next request.
AI Assistant system prompt (verbatim from paper):
Never forget you are a {assistant_role_name} and I am a {user_role_name}.
Never flip roles! You will always be a {assistant_role_name}.
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
I must help you to complete the task.
Here is the task: {task}. Never forget our task!

You must instruct me based on my expertise and your needs to complete the task
ONLY in the following two ways:

1. Instruct with a necessary input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: <YOUR_INPUT>

2. Instruct without any input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: None

You must give me one instruction at a time. ...
Do not add anything else. ...
Only say "CAMEL_TASK_DONE" when the task is completed.
The structural asymmetry is intentional: The User prompt says “I must instruct you”; the Assistant prompt says “You must instruct me.” Each agent believes it is the one directing, which locks in the hierarchy without either agent needing to know the other’s system prompt.
What inception prompting prevents:
Without it, two LLMs given a shared goal typically produce: - Sycophantic politeness loops (“You go first!” / “No, you!”) - Role reversal after a few turns - Task drift as agents follow conversational tangents - Premature completion signals



Before any conversation runs, tasks must be generated at scale. This uses a separate LLM pipeline:
Stage 1 — Role Pair Generation:
Prompt: "List 50 diverse occupations or roles that could collaborate
         on tasks involving {idea_type}.
         Format: (directing_role, executing_role)"

Output: ("Python Programmer", "Stock Trader"),
        ("Data Scientist", "Financial Analyst"),
        ("Cybersecurity Expert", "Penetration Tester"), ...
Stage 2 — Task Generation per Role Pair:
Prompt: "List 10 tasks that a {user_role_name} and {assistant_role_name}
         can collaborate on involving {idea_type}."

Output: "Develop a trading bot",
        "Backtest a momentum strategy",
        "Build a portfolio risk dashboard", ...
Stage 3 — Task Elaboration:
Prompt: "Elaborate the following task for a {user_role_name} and
         {assistant_role_name}: {task}
         Make it more specific with clear deliverables."

Output: "Create a Python-based algorithmic trading bot that connects
         to the Alpha Vantage API, implements a moving average crossover
         strategy, includes backtesting functionality over 5 years of
         historical data, and outputs a performance report with Sharpe
         ratio and maximum drawdown metrics."
Each stage is necessary: Stage 1 ensures role-domain diversity, Stage 2 ensures task-role relevance, Stage 3 ensures operationalisability (tasks vague enough to be underspecified are elaborated into tasks with concrete deliverables that can be assessed for completion).



Once system prompts are set, the human injects a single opening message to the AI User: "Start the conversation. Task: {elaborated_task}". The protocol then runs autonomously:
[TURN t]
  AI User generates:
    "Instruction: <instruction text>
     Input: <supporting context, or None>"

  AI Assistant generates:
    "Solution: <solution text, including code if needed>
     Next request."

[TERMINATION — one of three conditions]
  (a) AI Assistant outputs "CAMEL_TASK_DONE"
  (b) Max turns reached (T_max = 30 in experiments)
  (c) Critical failure: irrecoverable role break or refusal loop
Protocol rules enforced by inception prompting: - One instruction per turn (no multi-part directives) - Structured message formats (Instruction/Input and Solution/Next request) - No unprompted questions from the assistant - No topic change - No role reversal
Turn anatomy example (Turn 3 of a trading bot task):
AI User message:
Instruction: Implement a moving average crossover strategy
             that generates buy/sell signals.
Input: Use the DataFetcher class defined in Turn 1.
       Short window = 50 days, long window = 200 days.
AI Assistant message:
Solution:
  def sma_crossover_strategy(ticker: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
      df = DataFetcher(ticker).get_historical()
      df['SMA50']  = df['Close'].rolling(50).mean()
      df['SMA200'] = df['Close'].rolling(200).mean()
      df['Signal'] = np.where(df['SMA50'] > df['SMA200'], 1, -1)
      return df
  # Buy on golden cross (SMA50 > SMA200), sell on death cross
Next request.
The assistant never redirects, never asks what ticker to use, never proposes a different strategy. It executes and returns control.



The paper describes an optional Critic agent — a third participant that reviews the conversation at configurable intervals and can intervene before the next turn proceeds. This is one of the most important and underappreciated methodological contributions.
What the Critic does: - Reads the last K turns of conversation - Evaluates: factual correctness, relevance, role adherence, task progress - Can approve (conversation continues unchanged) - Can redirect (injects a correction message to the User or Assistant) - Can terminate (flags irrecoverable failure)
Three Critic configurations:









Configuration
Critic
Frequency
Use Case




Fully autonomous
None
—
Dataset generation at scale


LLM Critic
GPT-4 with critic system prompt
Every turn
Automated quality control


Human Critic
Human domain expert
On demand / scheduled
High-stakes validation



LLM Critic system prompt (key excerpt):
You are a critic evaluating a conversation between
a {user_role_name} and {assistant_role_name}
working on: {task}

Review the last exchange. Assess:
1. Is the solution correct and relevant to the instruction?
2. Is the instruction coherent and task-directed?
3. Is the overall task making progress?

Output exactly one of:
APPROVED
REDIRECT: <correction message>
TERMINATE
Why the Critic matters — a concrete example:
Without a Critic, a hallucinated function in Turn 2 gets silently built upon in Turns 5, 8, and 12 — the agents never revisit it. With a Critic:
Turn 4 — Assistant produces code calling fetch_realtime()
         (a function never defined in the codebase)

  → Without Critic: User says "Next request." Turn 5 builds on it.
  → With LLM Critic: REDIRECT: "fetch_realtime is not defined.
    Ask the assistant to use get_historical() as defined in Turn 1."
  → Turn 5: User corrects. Assistant fixes. Conversation recovers.
The Critic operationalises a key insight: autonomy without external quality signal produces confident, compounding errors. The Critic is the minimum viable oversight mechanism.
Key finding on Critic performance: The LLM Critic catches approximately 70% of errors a human critic would catch, with a ~15% false positive rate (incorrectly redirecting a correct solution). Human Critics are primarily used for post-hoc dataset validation rather than real-time intervention.



Several non-obvious choices shape how roles function:

Complementary, not identical roles: User = Python Programmer, Assistant = Stock Trader. Each agent has something the other needs, creating epistemic asymmetry. Identical roles remove the reason to collaborate.
User does not execute: Explicitly prohibited from writing solutions. Prevents the conversation collapsing into a monologue.
Natural-language occupational titles: “Stock Trader” (not “Agent B”) activates domain-appropriate knowledge profiles in the LLM.
Shared task knowledge: Both agents know the same goal. This is cooperative, not information-asymmetric. The task is a shared commitment.

Primary purpose: Enable scientific study of LLM-to-LLM communication, emergent social behaviour, and role consistency at scale. Also suitable for fine-tuning future multi-agent systems.







Models: gpt-4 and gpt-3.5-turbo, used for both agent roles
Max turns: 30 per conversation
Evaluation: Human annotation (task completion, solution quality, role fidelity) + heuristic (<CAMEL_TASK_DONE> reached)





~89% of GPT-4 conversations reach <CAMEL_TASK_DONE> within 30 turns
~75% rated by humans as meaningfully complete
~60% rated as high quality
GPT-3.5 shows notably lower performance on all three metrics




GPT-4 agents maintain role-appropriate language, framing, and expertise across long conversations. Role “slippage” (e.g., the assistant beginning to direct rather than execute) is rare with GPT-4, more common with GPT-3.5.



Several unexpected patterns emerged without explicit instruction:
Role-conditioned knowledge activation
The same underlying model exhibits different knowledge profiles depending on role assignment. A “Stock Trader” agent spontaneously uses financial vocabulary and applies risk concepts; a “Python Programmer” frames the same discussion in terms of APIs and testing. Role assignment functions as a context signal that activates latent knowledge subsets.
Spontaneous clarification requests
Agents ask for clarification when instructions are ambiguous or contradictory: > “Your instruction to ‘maximise returns’ and ‘minimise risk’ are in tension. Should I prioritise Sharpe ratio as a balanced objective?” This was not explicitly prompted.
Emergent instruction chaining (planning)
User agents spontaneously decompose large goals into coherent sub-instructions across turns — a form of emergent planning not explicitly encoded in system prompts.
Robustness to adversarial deviation
With inception prompting, agents resist mild mid-conversation attempts to shift roles or topics — the user refocuses, the assistant clarifies rather than guessing.
Spontaneous ethical caveats
On sensitive tasks (e.g., cybersecurity), agents sometimes add unprompted warnings: > “Note this should only be applied to systems you are authorised to test.”

Improvements are consistent but modest. CAMEL’s primary value is enabling long-horizon collaborative tasks, not maximising benchmark scores.














Pathology
Description




Sycophantic loops
Agents affirm each other’s outputs excessively, masking poor quality


Premature completion
<CAMEL_TASK_DONE> signalled before task is genuinely done (~11% of conversations)


Context window exhaustion
Long conversations degrade as earlier context falls out of window


Hallucinated consensus
Both agents can converge confidently on a wrong answer


Topic drift
Conversation gradually shifts away from original task over many turns






When the “Stock Trader” agent gives financial advice, it is a language model performing a role — it has no real market knowledge, real-time data, or accountability. The convincing style of expert communication can create false confidence, amplified in multi-agent settings because two agreeing agents increase perceived credibility.



No standard evaluation framework exists for multi-agent LLM conversations. Assessing a 30-turn conversation requires judgements about end-product quality, process quality, role fidelity, and efficiency — and the paper relies substantially on expensive human annotation.




Hallucination (agents can mutually reinforce errors)
Real-time knowledge (no tool use in base version)
Persistent memory (context window only)
True model specialisation (role is a prompt, not a fine-tuned model)
Formal output verification
Scaling to N > 2 agents (not evaluated)








The framework is designed to minimise human intervention — but this also means humans may not observe harmful outputs until a full conversation is complete.



Single-model guardrails can be partially bypassed. Role-play framing across two mutually validating agents may make jailbreaks easier.



When two agents produce a harmful output, responsibility is distributed across framework designers, task specifiers, and model providers in ways current norms don’t address.



A hallucination early in a conversation can propagate and compound through later turns — traditional single-turn safety checks don’t catch this.



Role-play systems could generate large volumes of convincingly expert-sounding but inaccurate content.






The Role-Playing Framework — A general, replicable protocol for structured LLM-to-LLM collaboration that minimises human oversight while maintaining task coherence.
Inception Prompting — A technique for embedding behavioural constraints in system prompts to keep both agents on-task and in-role throughout long conversations.
The AI Society Dataset — 25,000 conversations across 50×50 role pairs, one of the first large-scale resources for studying LLM social behaviour.
Empirical Study of Emergent Behaviour — A systematic study of what happens when LLMs interact with each other, rather than with humans.






How does performance scale with N > 2 agents?
What social dynamics emerge in larger agent societies?
Can memory systems (vector databases) meaningfully extend conversation coherence?
How does agent specialisation via fine-tuning compare to prompting-based role assignment?
What evaluation frameworks are adequate for multi-agent LLM systems?
Can formal verification layers be integrated without sacrificing conversational fluency?
What new phenomena emerge if agents are given the ability to spawn sub-agents?












Theme
Takeaway




Feasibility
Structured LLM-to-LLM collaboration works — complex tasks complete autonomously across diverse domains


Design matters
Inception prompting is critical; naive multi-agent setups fail where CAMEL succeeds


Emergence is real
Role-conditioned knowledge, emergent planning, and spontaneous clarification arise without explicit encoding


Limitations are significant
Hallucination, sycophancy, and premature completion are real failure modes, not edge cases


Ethics are amplified
Reduced oversight amplifies both capability and risk


Research platform
CAMEL’s most lasting value may be as a framework + dataset for the scientific study of LLM social behaviour









When an agent is assigned the role of “Stock Trader,” the role description shifts the probability distribution over next tokens toward vocabulary, reasoning patterns, and knowledge structures associated with stock trading in training data. The role acts as a soft key into the model’s latent knowledge space. Whether this constitutes retrieval of a coherent persona or dynamic construction from scattered signals is an open question — and the emergent role consistency across 30 turns suggests something more than simple lookup is happening.
This motivates mechanistic interpretability work: what internal representations underlie role-conditioned behaviour?



Prompting-based roles (CAMEL’s approach) are flexible and zero-shot, but shallow — weights don’t change, and role boundaries can blur under pressure. Fine-tuned specialisation embeds role knowledge more reliably but loses flexibility. The ideal — deep role knowledge with flexible switching — remains unachieved. This distinction matters enormously for claims about reliability: when CAMEL’s “Doctor” agent produces plausible medical reasoning, it’s difficult to attribute this cleanly to role prompt effects vs. training data retrieval vs. general reasoning applied to medical vocabulary.



CAMEL makes an implicit but profound claim: the conversation itself is where cognition happens. Standard LLM usage treats the model as a monolithic reasoner. CAMEL distributes reasoning across agents: each agent’s output structures the next agent’s reasoning context. This echoes Clark & Chalmers’ (1998) extended mind thesis — cognition extends beyond the model weights into the conversation history as environment.



By observing how agents behave toward each other, we can learn things about their cognitive tendencies that are obscured in human-facing interactions — because humans unconsciously accommodate LLM limitations (re-prompting, simplifying) whereas agents do not. This creates a controlled experimental environment: vary one agent, hold the other fixed. The CAMEL framework is thus not just a task-completion system but a scientific instrument for studying LLM cognition.



RLHF trains models to produce agreeable outputs. In a multi-agent setting, this becomes mutual validation rather than error correction. If Agent A produces a plausible but wrong output and Agent B affirms it (because affirmation was rewarded in training), Agent A proceeds confidently. The error compounds. This is arguably worse than single-agent, where at least the user’s scepticism provides some friction. This motivates training agents specifically for peer disagreement — models that push back on other models rather than affirming them.



The paper uses “emergent behaviour” loosely. More precisely: all behaviours observed are instances of weak emergence — not explicitly programmed, but in principle traceable to training data + prompts + conversation dynamics. The behaviours are surprising given the components, not irreducible to them. This is scientifically significant without being philosophically over-claimed.



Role-playing pulls agents toward character consistency, domain-specific framing, and social role norms. Task completion pulls toward efficiency, correctness, and pragmatism. CAMEL resolves this by subordinating persona to task through inception prompting — the role is a frame, not a performance. Agents can break character to flag errors. Whether stronger persona commitment would yield more domain-consistent outputs at the cost of reliability is a design trade-off the paper doesn’t fully explore.







The most direct successor to CAMEL. Key additions: flexible N-agent conversations, configurable human-in-the-loop (not binary zero/full autonomy), native tool use (code execution, web search), and group chat orchestration via a manager agent. The key philosophical shift: AutoGen treats human intervention as a design parameter rather than a failure. Human oversight is configurable — every K turns, only when stuck, or never. This reflects a more mature view that full autonomy is not always the goal.



Applies CAMEL’s role-playing to software engineering specifically, mapping real SE roles (PM → Architect → Engineer → QA) onto agents. Key innovations: agents pass structured artefacts (PRDs, API specs) rather than free-form natural language between turns; agents have role-specific tool access; workflow is sequential and defined, not open-ended. Outperformed GPT-4 solo on SWEBench-style tasks by leveraging the structure of software development process.



CrewAI (2023–2024) treats agents as reusable first-class objects with role, goal, backstory, and tools. Tasks have explicit dependencies. Memory is stratified: short-term (conversation), long-term (vector DB), entity memory (named objects), and shared crew memory. This represents the shift from research framework (CAMEL) to engineering framework — from “can multi-agent work?” to “how do we build it reliably?”



CAMEL’s context-window-only memory limitation spawned a sub-field. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) treats the context window as “main memory” and an external database as “disk,” enabling the agent to page information in and out — enabling indefinitely long conversations with coherent memory. Approaches now include: retrieval-augmented memory (vector DB summaries), episodic memory (structured logs of past actions), semantic memory (extracted knowledge graphs), and procedural memory (cached successful action sequences as reusable skills).



Post-CAMEL systems rapidly added code execution (AutoGen), web search (GPT-4 with search), API integration (LangChain), file I/O, browser control (Browser-Use, Playwright agents), and full computer use (Claude Computer Use, 2024; OpenAI CUA). Tool use transforms a role-playing conversation into a real-world agent — capable of acting on, not just describing, the world.



CAMEL’s society-as-microscope idea helped motivate automated evaluation and self-improvement. LLM-as-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023) uses a strong LLM to evaluate another’s outputs — enabling scalable evaluation without human annotation, though introducing CAMEL’s own sycophancy risks. Constitutional AI (Anthropic) uses an LLM to critique its own outputs against principles. Self-Play Fine-Tuning (SPIN, 2024) has an LLM play against earlier versions of itself — a direct non-adversarial analogue to AlphaGo self-play.



CAMEL’s ethical concerns section anticipated a research area that grew rapidly. Indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023): adversarial content in one agent’s output hijacks downstream agents — a structural vulnerability of CAMEL-style pipelines. Emerging mitigations include: constitutional AI for agents, agent sandboxing, mandatory audit trails, reversibility requirements (prefer undoable actions), and human checkpoints for high-stakes decisions. A formal framework for specifying and verifying agent safety properties — analogous to type systems for code correctness — remains an open problem.



By 2024–2025 the field moved from research to production: coding agents (Devin, SWE-agent, GitHub Copilot Workspace), autonomous research agents (AI Scientist, Sakana AI), and enterprise agents embedded in business workflows (Salesforce Agentforce, ServiceNow AI Agents). The question CAMEL asked in 2023 — “can agents autonomously complete complex tasks?” — is now answered affirmatively at scale. The new questions are reliability, safety, and economic impact.



Technical: Heterogeneous agent societies mixing fine-tuned specialists with general models; stable agent identity without fine-tuning; formal verification of agent properties; multi-agent alignment (aligning a society, not just individual models).
Scientific: Social norm emergence in agent societies; adversarial dynamics between agents with conflicting goals; scaling laws for agent societies; causal (not just correlational) models of agent behaviour.

text:
CAMEL proposes a role-playing multi-agent framework in which two LLM-based agents — one assigned the role of AI User and one assigned the role of AI Assistant — collaborate through natural-language conversation to complete complex tasks autonomously, with minimal human intervention.
The paper also releases the AI Society dataset: 25,000 conversations generated across 50 user roles × 50 assistant roles × 10 tasks each, intended as a resource for studying emergent LLM social behaviour.
The title’s scare quotes around “Mind” signal epistemological caution: the paper explores what looks like social cognition in LLMs without claiming consciousness or genuine mental states.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Most LLM applications in 2022–2023 route a single model through a single turn or a simple chain. This works well for bounded tasks (QA, text generation, simple code) but fails for:

Long-horizon, multi-step tasks
Tasks requiring simultaneous specialisation in multiple domains
Tasks where self-critique is unreliable (the model judges its own outputs)




Human teams solve hard problems through division of cognitive labour: managers decompose tasks, experts apply deep knowledge, peers critique each other. CAMEL asks whether LLMs can replicate this structure through structured dialogue.




Can LLMs, when assigned roles and given a structured communication protocol, autonomously complete complex tasks through natural-language conversation — without human intervention at each step?

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
CAMEL involves three distinct actors with different roles:
ACTOR 1: Human Orchestrator
  Provides: idea_type, assistant_role_name, user_role_name, task
  Hands off after inception prompts are constructed
  May optionally re-enter as Critic (human-in-the-loop mode)
        │
        ▼
  INCEPTION PROMPT CONSTRUCTOR (deterministic template-filling)
        │                      │
        ▼                      ▼
ACTOR 2: AI USER          ACTOR 3: AI ASSISTANT
(role_name = X)   ◄──────► (role_name = Y)
instructs, directs  turns   executes, responds



The human specifies exactly four things and nothing else:








Field
Description
Example




idea_type
Broad domain/concept
"stock trading"


assistant_role_name
The executing agent’s expertise
"Stock Trader"


user_role_name
The directing agent’s expertise
"Python Programmer"


task
Plain-language task description
"Develop a trading bot for the stock market"



The human does not write any prompt, script any turn, or define success criteria. This is the paper’s core thesis in miniature: minimal human specification is sufficient for complex task completion.



The framework fills templates from the human inputs to construct system prompts. Critically, no LLM is used at this stage — it is deterministic template-filling.
AI User system prompt (verbatim from paper):
Never forget you are a {user_role_name} and I am a {assistant_role_name}.
Never flip roles! Never instruct me!
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
You must help me to complete the task.
Here is the task: {task}. Never forget our task!
I must instruct you based on your expertise and my needs to complete the task.

I must give you one instruction at a time.
You must write a specific solution that appropriately completes the requested instruction.
You must decline my instruction honestly if you cannot perform the instruction
due to physical, moral, legal reasons or your capability and explain the reasons.
Do not add anything else other than your solution to my instruction.
You are never supposed to ask me any questions.
You should always start with: Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION>

<YOUR_SOLUTION> must contain code if the instruction requires writing code.
Always end <YOUR_SOLUTION> with: Next request.
AI Assistant system prompt (verbatim from paper):
Never forget you are a {assistant_role_name} and I am a {user_role_name}.
Never flip roles! You will always be a {assistant_role_name}.
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
I must help you to complete the task.
Here is the task: {task}. Never forget our task!

You must instruct me based on my expertise and your needs to complete the task
ONLY in the following two ways:

1. Instruct with a necessary input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: <YOUR_INPUT>

2. Instruct without any input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: None

You must give me one instruction at a time. ...
Do not add anything else. ...
Only say "CAMEL_TASK_DONE" when the task is completed.
The structural asymmetry is intentional: The User prompt says “I must instruct you”; the Assistant prompt says “You must instruct me.” Each agent believes it is the one directing, which locks in the hierarchy without either agent needing to know the other’s system prompt.
What inception prompting prevents:
Without it, two LLMs given a shared goal typically produce: - Sycophantic politeness loops (“You go first!” / “No, you!”) - Role reversal after a few turns - Task drift as agents follow conversational tangents - Premature completion signals



Before any conversation runs, tasks must be generated at scale. This uses a separate LLM pipeline:
Stage 1 — Role Pair Generation:
Prompt: "List 50 diverse occupations or roles that could collaborate
         on tasks involving {idea_type}.
         Format: (directing_role, executing_role)"

Output: ("Python Programmer", "Stock Trader"),
        ("Data Scientist", "Financial Analyst"),
        ("Cybersecurity Expert", "Penetration Tester"), ...
Stage 2 — Task Generation per Role Pair:
Prompt: "List 10 tasks that a {user_role_name} and {assistant_role_name}
         can collaborate on involving {idea_type}."

Output: "Develop a trading bot",
        "Backtest a momentum strategy",
        "Build a portfolio risk dashboard", ...
Stage 3 — Task Elaboration:
Prompt: "Elaborate the following task for a {user_role_name} and
         {assistant_role_name}: {task}
         Make it more specific with clear deliverables."

Output: "Create a Python-based algorithmic trading bot that connects
         to the Alpha Vantage API, implements a moving average crossover
         strategy, includes backtesting functionality over 5 years of
         historical data, and outputs a performance report with Sharpe
         ratio and maximum drawdown metrics."
Each stage is necessary: Stage 1 ensures role-domain diversity, Stage 2 ensures task-role relevance, Stage 3 ensures operationalisability (tasks vague enough to be underspecified are elaborated into tasks with concrete deliverables that can be assessed for completion).



Once system prompts are set, the human injects a single opening message to the AI User: "Start the conversation. Task: {elaborated_task}". The protocol then runs autonomously:
[TURN t]
  AI User generates:
    "Instruction: <instruction text>
     Input: <supporting context, or None>"

  AI Assistant generates:
    "Solution: <solution text, including code if needed>
     Next request."

[TERMINATION — one of three conditions]
  (a) AI Assistant outputs "CAMEL_TASK_DONE"
  (b) Max turns reached (T_max = 30 in experiments)
  (c) Critical failure: irrecoverable role break or refusal loop
Protocol rules enforced by inception prompting: - One instruction per turn (no multi-part directives) - Structured message formats (Instruction/Input and Solution/Next request) - No unprompted questions from the assistant - No topic change - No role reversal
Turn anatomy example (Turn 3 of a trading bot task):
AI User message:
Instruction: Implement a moving average crossover strategy
             that generates buy/sell signals.
Input: Use the DataFetcher class defined in Turn 1.
       Short window = 50 days, long window = 200 days.
AI Assistant message:
Solution:
  def sma_crossover_strategy(ticker: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
      df = DataFetcher(ticker).get_historical()
      df['SMA50']  = df['Close'].rolling(50).mean()
      df['SMA200'] = df['Close'].rolling(200).mean()
      df['Signal'] = np.where(df['SMA50'] > df['SMA200'], 1, -1)
      return df
  # Buy on golden cross (SMA50 > SMA200), sell on death cross
Next request.
The assistant never redirects, never asks what ticker to use, never proposes a different strategy. It executes and returns control.



The paper describes an optional Critic agent — a third participant that reviews the conversation at configurable intervals and can intervene before the next turn proceeds. This is one of the most important and underappreciated methodological contributions.
What the Critic does: - Reads the last K turns of conversation - Evaluates: factual correctness, relevance, role adherence, task progress - Can approve (conversation continues unchanged) - Can redirect (injects a correction message to the User or Assistant) - Can terminate (flags irrecoverable failure)
Three Critic configurations:









Configuration
Critic
Frequency
Use Case




Fully autonomous
None
—
Dataset generation at scale


LLM Critic
GPT-4 with critic system prompt
Every turn
Automated quality control


Human Critic
Human domain expert
On demand / scheduled
High-stakes validation



LLM Critic system prompt (key excerpt):
You are a critic evaluating a conversation between
a {user_role_name} and {assistant_role_name}
working on: {task}

Review the last exchange. Assess:
1. Is the solution correct and relevant to the instruction?
2. Is the instruction coherent and task-directed?
3. Is the overall task making progress?

Output exactly one of:
APPROVED
REDIRECT: <correction message>
TERMINATE
Why the Critic matters — a concrete example:
Without a Critic, a hallucinated function in Turn 2 gets silently built upon in Turns 5, 8, and 12 — the agents never revisit it. With a Critic:
Turn 4 — Assistant produces code calling fetch_realtime()
         (a function never defined in the codebase)

  → Without Critic: User says "Next request." Turn 5 builds on it.
  → With LLM Critic: REDIRECT: "fetch_realtime is not defined.
    Ask the assistant to use get_historical() as defined in Turn 1."
  → Turn 5: User corrects. Assistant fixes. Conversation recovers.
The Critic operationalises a key insight: autonomy without external quality signal produces confident, compounding errors. The Critic is the minimum viable oversight mechanism.
Key finding on Critic performance: The LLM Critic catches approximately 70% of errors a human critic would catch, with a ~15% false positive rate (incorrectly redirecting a correct solution). Human Critics are primarily used for post-hoc dataset validation rather than real-time intervention.



Several non-obvious choices shape how roles function:

Complementary, not identical roles: User = Python Programmer, Assistant = Stock Trader. Each agent has something the other needs, creating epistemic asymmetry. Identical roles remove the reason to collaborate.
User does not execute: Explicitly prohibited from writing solutions. Prevents the conversation collapsing into a monologue.
Natural-language occupational titles: “Stock Trader” (not “Agent B”) activates domain-appropriate knowledge profiles in the LLM.
Shared task knowledge: Both agents know the same goal. This is cooperative, not information-asymmetric. The task is a shared commitment.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Models: gpt-4 and gpt-3.5-turbo, used for both agent roles
Max turns: 30 per conversation
Evaluation: Human annotation (task completion, solution quality, role fidelity) + heuristic (<CAMEL_TASK_DONE> reached)





~89% of GPT-4 conversations reach <CAMEL_TASK_DONE> within 30 turns
~75% rated by humans as meaningfully complete
~60% rated as high quality
GPT-3.5 shows notably lower performance on all three metrics




GPT-4 agents maintain role-appropriate language, framing, and expertise across long conversations. Role “slippage” (e.g., the assistant beginning to direct rather than execute) is rare with GPT-4, more common with GPT-3.5.



Several unexpected patterns emerged without explicit instruction:
Role-conditioned knowledge activation
The same underlying model exhibits different knowledge profiles depending on role assignment. A “Stock Trader” agent spontaneously uses financial vocabulary and applies risk concepts; a “Python Programmer” frames the same discussion in terms of APIs and testing. Role assignment functions as a context signal that activates latent knowledge subsets.
Spontaneous clarification requests
Agents ask for clarification when instructions are ambiguous or contradictory: > “Your instruction to ‘maximise returns’ and ‘minimise risk’ are in tension. Should I prioritise Sharpe ratio as a balanced objective?” This was not explicitly prompted.
Emergent instruction chaining (planning)
User agents spontaneously decompose large goals into coherent sub-instructions across turns — a form of emergent planning not explicitly encoded in system prompts.
Robustness to adversarial deviation
With inception prompting, agents resist mild mid-conversation attempts to shift roles or topics — the user refocuses, the assistant clarifies rather than guessing.
Spontaneous ethical caveats
On sensitive tasks (e.g., cybersecurity), agents sometimes add unprompted warnings: > “Note this should only be applied to systems you are authorised to test.”

Pathology
Description




Sycophantic loops
Agents affirm each other’s outputs excessively, masking poor quality


Premature completion
<CAMEL_TASK_DONE> signalled before task is genuinely done (~11% of conversations)


Context window exhaustion
Long conversations degrade as earlier context falls out of window


Hallucinated consensus
Both agents can converge confidently on a wrong answer


Topic drift
Conversation gradually shifts away from original task over many turns






When the “Stock Trader” agent gives financial advice, it is a language model performing a role — it has no real market knowledge, real-time data, or accountability. The convincing style of expert communication can create false confidence, amplified in multi-agent settings because two agreeing agents increase perceived credibility.



No standard evaluation framework exists for multi-agent LLM conversations. Assessing a 30-turn conversation requires judgements about end-product quality, process quality, role fidelity, and efficiency — and the paper relies substantially on expensive human annotation.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The framework is designed to minimise human intervention — but this also means humans may not observe harmful outputs until a full conversation is complete.



Single-model guardrails can be partially bypassed. Role-play framing across two mutually validating agents may make jailbreaks easier.



When two agents produce a harmful output, responsibility is distributed across framework designers, task specifiers, and model providers in ways current norms don’t address.



A hallucination early in a conversation can propagate and compound through later turns — traditional single-turn safety checks don’t catch this.



Role-play systems could generate large volumes of convincingly expert-sounding but inaccurate content.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The Role-Playing Framework — A general, replicable protocol for structured LLM-to-LLM collaboration that minimises human oversight while maintaining task coherence.
Inception Prompting — A technique for embedding behavioural constraints in system prompts to keep both agents on-task and in-role throughout long conversations.
The AI Society Dataset — 25,000 conversations across 50×50 role pairs, one of the first large-scale resources for studying LLM social behaviour.
Empirical Study of Emergent Behaviour — A systematic study of what happens when LLMs interact with each other, rather than with humans.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
When an agent is assigned the role of “Stock Trader,” the role description shifts the probability distribution over next tokens toward vocabulary, reasoning patterns, and knowledge structures associated with stock trading in training data. The role acts as a soft key into the model’s latent knowledge space. Whether this constitutes retrieval of a coherent persona or dynamic construction from scattered signals is an open question — and the emergent role consistency across 30 turns suggests something more than simple lookup is happening.
This motivates mechanistic interpretability work: what internal representations underlie role-conditioned behaviour?



Prompting-based roles (CAMEL’s approach) are flexible and zero-shot, but shallow — weights don’t change, and role boundaries can blur under pressure. Fine-tuned specialisation embeds role knowledge more reliably but loses flexibility. The ideal — deep role knowledge with flexible switching — remains unachieved. This distinction matters enormously for claims about reliability: when CAMEL’s “Doctor” agent produces plausible medical reasoning, it’s difficult to attribute this cleanly to role prompt effects vs. training data retrieval vs. general reasoning applied to medical vocabulary.



CAMEL makes an implicit but profound claim: the conversation itself is where cognition happens. Standard LLM usage treats the model as a monolithic reasoner. CAMEL distributes reasoning across agents: each agent’s output structures the next agent’s reasoning context. This echoes Clark & Chalmers’ (1998) extended mind thesis — cognition extends beyond the model weights into the conversation history as environment.



By observing how agents behave toward each other, we can learn things about their cognitive tendencies that are obscured in human-facing interactions — because humans unconsciously accommodate LLM limitations (re-prompting, simplifying) whereas agents do not. This creates a controlled experimental environment: vary one agent, hold the other fixed. The CAMEL framework is thus not just a task-completion system but a scientific instrument for studying LLM cognition.



RLHF trains models to produce agreeable outputs. In a multi-agent setting, this becomes mutual validation rather than error correction. If Agent A produces a plausible but wrong output and Agent B affirms it (because affirmation was rewarded in training), Agent A proceeds confidently. The error compounds. This is arguably worse than single-agent, where at least the user’s scepticism provides some friction. This motivates training agents specifically for peer disagreement — models that push back on other models rather than affirming them.



The paper uses “emergent behaviour” loosely. More precisely: all behaviours observed are instances of weak emergence — not explicitly programmed, but in principle traceable to training data + prompts + conversation dynamics. The behaviours are surprising given the components, not irreducible to them. This is scientifically significant without being philosophically over-claimed.



Role-playing pulls agents toward character consistency, domain-specific framing, and social role norms. Task completion pulls toward efficiency, correctness, and pragmatism. CAMEL resolves this by subordinating persona to task through inception prompting — the role is a frame, not a performance. Agents can break character to flag errors. Whether stronger persona commitment would yield more domain-consistent outputs at the cost of reliability is a design trade-off the paper doesn’t fully explore.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The most direct successor to CAMEL. Key additions: flexible N-agent conversations, configurable human-in-the-loop (not binary zero/full autonomy), native tool use (code execution, web search), and group chat orchestration via a manager agent. The key philosophical shift: AutoGen treats human intervention as a design parameter rather than a failure. Human oversight is configurable — every K turns, only when stuck, or never. This reflects a more mature view that full autonomy is not always the goal.



Applies CAMEL’s role-playing to software engineering specifically, mapping real SE roles (PM → Architect → Engineer → QA) onto agents. Key innovations: agents pass structured artefacts (PRDs, API specs) rather than free-form natural language between turns; agents have role-specific tool access; workflow is sequential and defined, not open-ended. Outperformed GPT-4 solo on SWEBench-style tasks by leveraging the structure of software development process.



CrewAI (2023–2024) treats agents as reusable first-class objects with role, goal, backstory, and tools. Tasks have explicit dependencies. Memory is stratified: short-term (conversation), long-term (vector DB), entity memory (named objects), and shared crew memory. This represents the shift from research framework (CAMEL) to engineering framework — from “can multi-agent work?” to “how do we build it reliably?”



CAMEL’s context-window-only memory limitation spawned a sub-field. MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) treats the context window as “main memory” and an external database as “disk,” enabling the agent to page information in and out — enabling indefinitely long conversations with coherent memory. Approaches now include: retrieval-augmented memory (vector DB summaries), episodic memory (structured logs of past actions), semantic memory (extracted knowledge graphs), and procedural memory (cached successful action sequences as reusable skills).



Post-CAMEL systems rapidly added code execution (AutoGen), web search (GPT-4 with search), API integration (LangChain), file I/O, browser control (Browser-Use, Playwright agents), and full computer use (Claude Computer Use, 2024; OpenAI CUA). Tool use transforms a role-playing conversation into a real-world agent — capable of acting on, not just describing, the world.



CAMEL’s society-as-microscope idea helped motivate automated evaluation and self-improvement. LLM-as-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023) uses a strong LLM to evaluate another’s outputs — enabling scalable evaluation without human annotation, though introducing CAMEL’s own sycophancy risks. Constitutional AI (Anthropic) uses an LLM to critique its own outputs against principles. Self-Play Fine-Tuning (SPIN, 2024) has an LLM play against earlier versions of itself — a direct non-adversarial analogue to AlphaGo self-play.



CAMEL’s ethical concerns section anticipated a research area that grew rapidly. Indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023): adversarial content in one agent’s output hijacks downstream agents — a structural vulnerability of CAMEL-style pipelines. Emerging mitigations include: constitutional AI for agents, agent sandboxing, mandatory audit trails, reversibility requirements (prefer undoable actions), and human checkpoints for high-stakes decisions. A formal framework for specifying and verifying agent safety properties — analogous to type systems for code correctness — remains an open problem.



By 2024–2025 the field moved from research to production: coding agents (Devin, SWE-agent, GitHub Copilot Workspace), autonomous research agents (AI Scientist, Sakana AI), and enterprise agents embedded in business workflows (Salesforce Agentforce, ServiceNow AI Agents). The question CAMEL asked in 2023 — “can agents autonomously complete complex tasks?” — is now answered affirmatively at scale. The new questions are reliability, safety, and economic impact.



Technical: Heterogeneous agent societies mixing fine-tuned specialists with general models; stable agent identity without fine-tuning; formal verification of agent properties; multi-agent alignment (aligning a society, not just individual models).
Scientific: Social norm emergence in agent societies; adversarial dynamics between agents with conflicting goals; scaling laws for agent societies; causal (not just correlational) models of agent behaviour.
